content.title: Why is electrification so slow in the public sector?
content.description: Sweden's vehicle fleet is electrifying rapidly, but not everywhere. While businesses are transitioning quickly, the public sector is falling behind. Almost 9 out of 10 new company cars are plug-in vehicles. Central government, municipalities and regions barely reach half that share, and their proportion has even fallen this year.
content.extendedDescription:
Why is this? What are businesses doing that the public sector is not? How can the transition to electric cars accelerate, and will the new EU requirements in the Clean Vehicles Directive force more electric cars into the public sector?

Together with Volkswagen Finans, we examine differences between private individuals, businesses and the public sector. We take a closer look at the factors driving rapid electrification in businesses, such as focusing on total cost of ownership rather than purchase price.

The seminar also highlights structural conditions for the electric vehicle transition, from procurement rules to uncertainty about residual values and the effects of new EU requirements such as the Clean Vehicles Directive. What is needed to accelerate the transition of large public vehicle fleets?

content.title: When uncertainty slows sustainable procurement – how can guidance on equivalent labels help?
content.description: How can procurement regulations be used and developed to strengthen sustainable development through public purchasing? And how can greater clarity about equivalent labels make it easier to use sustainability labels in procurement?
content.extendedDescription:
Public procurement amounts to around SEK 1 000 billion annually and is one of society's most powerful tools for driving a sustainable transition. Yet the field is marked by legal uncertainty, particularly around the concept of 'equivalent labels'. Although legislation clearly states that equivalent labels must be accepted, both the EU procurement directives and Swedish legislation lack a clear, consistent definition.

In practice, this ambiguity sometimes leads procuring organisations to refrain from setting ambitious sustainability requirements, while also creating a risk that labels are accepted without actually meeting equivalent requirements.

Against this backdrop, the need for both legal clarification and practical guidance is growing. How can equivalence be assessed in practice? The seminar presents a new legal report analysing the concept and providing guidance on how organisations can act. We also share municipal examples and experiences.

content.title: We can detect lung cancer earlier – so why are we not doing it?
content.description: Despite clear evidence that a targeted national lung cancer screening programme could save around 500 lives annually, Sweden has not introduced one. Advanced technology that could improve diagnostics also exists. Why is implementation delayed, and what is needed for more equitable cancer care?
content.extendedDescription:
Thousands of people die from lung cancer in Sweden each year, often because the disease is detected too late.
Regional differences, fragmented procurement and a lack of national coordination create major variations in access to early diagnosis. The seminar explores why screening and modern diagnostic solutions are taking so long to introduce and what is needed for more equitable, effective cancer care throughout Sweden.
Evidence and capacity to detect lung cancer earlier and save lives already exist. Insufficient implementation is primarily a matter of governance, prioritisation and organisation. A more nationally coordinated strategy, including screening decisions and better coordinated procurement, is crucial to equal access to modern diagnostics.
The seminar is part of Swedish Medtech and Lif's joint Life Science Arena during Almedalsveckan 2026.

content.title: Assessing asylum claims based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression
content.description: How are cases assessed in Sweden when people cite sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression – LGBTQI – as grounds for asylum?
content.extendedDescription: Asylum grounds linked to sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression form a distinct category in asylum assessment because they are based on internal processes rather than external events. Assessing these grounds involves evaluating not only the credibility of a person's actions, but also their sexual orientation and identity. Applicants may therefore experience the investigations as intrusive and traumatising. The event will discuss Delmi's latest policy brief, written by Thomas Wimark. The brief examines how the likelihood of being granted asylum varies between different grounds for asylum and which factors influence approval rates.

content.title: Can Sweden afford to underestimate women's entrepreneurship?
content.description: Sweden faces low growth, increased global competition and a growing need to strengthen innovation and competitiveness. At the same time, major differences between women and men remain in entrepreneurship and access to capital.
content.extendedDescription:
Only three in ten businesses are run by women, and as little as 1–2.5 per cent of venture capital goes to companies founded by women. This risks holding back entrepreneurship, investment and Sweden's long-term competitiveness.

SPP and Almi invite you to a breakfast discussion about entrepreneurship and women's access to capital. This panel discusses capital provision, risk, security and the structures that affect women's opportunities to develop businesses.

What is needed for capital to reach more people? How can financing, advisory services and social protection systems be developed to better support women entrepreneurs? And what role can banks, public bodies and pension capital play in contributing to more gender-equal entrepreneurship and strengthening Sweden's long-term competitiveness?

content.title: Voluntary return migration to Syria: return aspirations among Syrians living in Sweden and the EU
content.description: What do we actually know about return aspirations among Syrians living in Sweden and across the European Union?
content.extendedDescription: The fall of the Assad regime in December 2024 and the end of the Syrian civil war, which lasted more than 13 years, are said to have marked a decisive turning point for Syrians who sought protection in the European Union (EU), with many hoping to return and rebuild their country of origin. In 2025, against the backdrop of the civil war's end, the Swedish government tasked Migrationsverket with assessing the measures needed ahead of a possible increase in returns to Syria. However, Syria remains in a state of deep political uncertainty. Its fragile transition has the potential to shape the country's future and therefore the return aspirations of Syrians living abroad. The event will discuss Delmi's latest policy brief, written by Anna Hammarstedt. The brief aims to improve understanding of current return aspirations among Syrians living in Sweden and the EU.

content.title: Is today's EU what we voted for in 1994?
content.description: In 1994, Sweden voted for expanded trade and to work for a better Europe together with other EU countries. Since then, membership has prompted critical debate about increased centralisation challenging both Swedish self-government and prosperity.
content.extendedDescription: According to SCB's latest survey (May 2025), around 35% of voters oppose or are uncertain about Swedish EU membership (11% oppose and 24% are uncertain). They represent around 3 million voters who are not represented by any existing parliamentary party. Meanwhile, debate about membership is virtually absent. This may help explain why turnout in the last two EU elections fell from 55 to 53 per cent. The seminar aims to raise Swedish EU membership in the ongoing election debate. Parallels will be drawn with the United Kingdom and Norway, two countries that have chosen to remain outside the EU. The panel examines aspects of membership rarely heard in public debate, as well as what Sweden should do to finally realise what its people once voted for.

content.title: 15 000 new jobs and better public health – is it possible?
content.description: Poor eating habits affect both individuals and society through poorer health and productivity. What if a reform could help more people eat better while creating thousands of entry-level jobs? It already exists in Europe. It is now high time for Sweden to introduce smart meal benefits too.
content.extendedDescription:
Did you know that three in ten employees cannot afford to eat lunch every day?
This is concerning because unhealthy eating habits are the second-largest risk factor for disease after tobacco. Research also shows that poor lunch habits have major consequences over time for everything from quality of life to sickness absence and productivity growth.
Rising food prices have also made meals a source of stress for many households. The government's temporary reduction in food VAT is a welcome step in the right direction, but what if there were a more cost-effective, long-term reform that could do everything from improving public health to strengthening the Swedish economy?
That reform already exists in several European countries – and has proved effective both in creating jobs and in revitalising the restaurant industry.
Join a seminar where experts and decision-makers discuss how tax-free and tax-deductible meal benefits can make a real difference – for individuals and society as a whole.

content.title: Everyone wants to come to Örebro – how can cities attract people and businesses amid growing competition?
content.description: As cities and regions compete ever more fiercely for investment, skills and new business establishments, local attractiveness becomes increasingly important. Businesses looking to expand or establish operations weigh a range of factors in their decisions.
content.extendedDescription:
For many places, this means not only providing the right conditions here and now, but also creating long-term environments where businesses can grow, collaborate and develop. In recent years, Örebro has strengthened its position as an attractive location in Sweden, with a central geographical position, a growing business community and strong partnerships between the municipality, academia and businesses. At the same time, competition between cities and regions is increasing, both nationally and internationally.

So what actually carries most weight when businesses choose where to invest? How can Örebro continue to enhance its appeal and attract more businesses to invest, establish operations and grow here?

This discussion brings together representatives of business, the public sector and academia to explore what is needed to create an even stronger investment climate and how we can jointly position Örebro in the growing competition for the businesses of the future.

content.title: Challenging the Norm: Business as a Catalyst for Societal Shifts
content.description: How are societal norms created, challenged, and changed? Alcohol has long been central to social life, yet growing demands for inclusion and wellbeing are reshaping expectations. Can businesses play a role in driving positive cultural change while remaining commercially successful?
content.extendedDescription:

content.title: Diversity – Sweden's most underestimated engine of growth
content.description: At a time when companies are pursuing innovation, skills and competitiveness, one of the greatest drivers of growth is already right in front of us, yet repeatedly overlooked: diversity.
content.extendedDescription:
Although many organisations say they work on inclusion, efforts often get stuck at values, policies and symbolic initiatives, without a clear link to business results.

This session challenges the view of diversity as a soft issue and shows why it is one of our most practical business strategies.

* What happens in organisations where everyone thinks alike?
* How do different perspectives affect innovation, risk assessment and decision-making?
* Why do so many companies fail to turn diversity into actual growth?

Using insights from a diversity perspective and real business cases, we explore how diversity of thought – differences in perspectives, experiences and motivations – can become a decisive competitive advantage.

We go beyond representation to discuss what really makes a difference: how organisations can understand, lead and use differences to produce results.

content.title: AI as a competitive strength – how do we build a resilient Nordic industry?
content.description: Nordic industry is under pressure from rapid AI development, geopolitical turmoil and intense global competition. How can we secure digital and industrial sovereignty, access to reliable infrastructure, and rules that both strengthen resilience and enable growth?
content.extendedDescription:
As AI becomes a cornerstone of the economy, Nordic industry risks falling behind – or becoming newly dependent on global technology giants. Securing long-term competitiveness requires robust AI ecosystems with access to secure data infrastructure, skills and capital, as well as clear rules governing how the technology is developed and used.

In this seminar, representatives of industry, politics and the technology sector discuss how the Nordic countries can move from primarily using AI to also shaping the conditions for its development, implementation and governance. We explore digital and industrial sovereignty, secure and sustainable infrastructure, the risk of new dependencies, and how regulation can support innovation instead of holding it back.

The audience will hear concrete examples of how the public sector and business can work together to build a resilient, values-driven AI-based industry that is strong in global competition.

content.title: The EU's new capacity regulation – an obstacle or opportunity for regional rail?
content.description: During the 2000s, contracted regional and commuter rail services have increased by as much as 130 per cent. Existing track capacity must be used more efficiently, but how should the new regulation be applied in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
Regional public transport authorities' investments in fast, efficient rail mean regional and commuter services now play a crucial role in expanding labour market regions and helping companies recruit appropriately skilled staff. To facilitate commuting and strengthen jobs and growth nationwide, the government and parliament should therefore invest in regional and commuter rail. New lines are necessary, but these services cannot wait for capacity expansion well into the 2030s or beyond. The seminar offers perspectives from Öresundståg and Trafikverket, among others.

content.title: Can transparency stop Trumpism?
content.description: Regeringskollen is a database intended to promote democracy, transparency and accountability by collecting government decisions and opposition proposals in a searchable database. Many decisions are made very quickly and forgotten — we want to build a collective memory and gather the facts.
content.extendedDescription:
As citizens, we can assess a government every four years. But we often forget what it has done. Where has the government invested and where has it cut back overall? What decisions have been made in areas such as democracy, culture, education, climate and taxation? And what proposals has the opposition made in those areas?

Many decisions and proposals proceed despite criticism from consultation bodies, experts and civil society. A shift is occurring in which experts' knowledge is ignored and journalism dismissed as politics. How does this affect democracy and opportunities for accountability?

This seminar explores the work of gathering information about political proposals and decisions, the difficulties of finding the right information and why transparency matters in a democratic society.

Coffee and vegetarian breakfast rolls will be served.

content.title: Parental alienation – the hippo in the nursery: an overlooked form of child abuse
content.description: Parental alienation is both scientifically documented and highly contested. Researchers and those affected describe clear and serious harm to children, while critics argue that the concept can be misused and sometimes deny its existence.
content.extendedDescription:
Parental alienation means that a child is manipulated by one parent into rejecting the other, with whom the child previously had a close relationship, without legitimate grounds for doing so. It is currently being researched as both child abuse and intimate partner violence. For children subjected to parental alienation to receive help and protection, social services, courts and others must be able to identify it and distinguish it from other forms of violence against children. At present, children subjected to parental alienation are often left to their fate with their abusers.

The seminar is led by Anna Lytsy, a journalist and author who has followed international research and knowledge development on parental alienation for more than ten years. Together with lawyer Christina Bergenstein, she wrote the book "Barn som tvingas välja bort en förälder. Föräldraalienation i Sverige: fakta, erfarenheter, rättsregler" (Norstedts Juridik, 2019 and 2023). Three parents who have lost their children through parental alienation will also be on stage.

content.title: Strengthen language and communication in the workplace

content.title: Strengthen language and communication in the workplace
content.description: Communication has always been a workplace challenge. This is even clearer now that more people in Sweden's labour market have Swedish neither as their first nor strongest language. Language is a working-environment issue. How is your workplace doing? How could it do better?
content.extendedDescription:
Language and communication are fundamental to a healthy workplace. Language is the key to individual participation and development. Effective communication is essential for an efficient, safe and inclusive workplace. Language support and development therefore need to be an integral part of working-environment efforts.

When employees lack the necessary language skills, insecurity, misunderstandings and ultimately exclusion from working life can result. This makes language both a working-environment issue and, ultimately, a public health issue.

How can we promote workplaces that develop language skills, where language and communication are a shared concern at individual, group and organisational level? This is one of the most important societal issues of our time and the future.

Tip! This session is a walk & talk. (We wait for participants at the meeting point for 15 minutes.) We walk together and explore how to strengthen language and communication at your workplace.

content.title: What will Sweden's future electricity system look like – and how do we get there?
content.description: The electricity system faces major changes, with development partly characterised by uncertainties and conflicting objectives. This requires clear priorities and shared responsibility.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar explores how planning can progress effectively, who has a role and what conditions enable success.

• How can we balance electricity generation and demand in the short and long term?
• Which decisions and investments should be prioritised today to avoid future capacity shortages?
• How can responsibility and collaboration between electricity system actors be strengthened to create a more efficient whole?
• How do spatial planning, environmental considerations and local decisions affect electricity system development?
• What roles should national, regional and local actors play in expanding a robust, sustainable electricity system?

content.title: Heta stubben: a boost for outdoor recreation through investment in nature and physical activity – the perfect recipe for sustainability?
content.description: Naturvårdsverket proposes doubling funding for organised outdoor recreation and substantially increasing funding for the management of valuable natural areas. Folkhälsomyndigheten wants a national initiative to increase physical activity, with outdoor recreation playing an important role. Is this the perfect recipe for sustainability?
content.extendedDescription:
Last year's Almedalen success, Heta stubben, is back. With the sea as a backdrop and the smell of coffee brewing on a camping stove, Friluftsfrämjandet will meet party leaders and other decision-makers on different occasions to discuss their vision for outdoor recreation. 94 per cent of Swedes believe that outdoor recreation benefits health and well-being. How can outdoor recreation have as natural a place in societal development as it does in our hearts? How can more people be encouraged to be active in nature?
Four in five children get too little physical activity, and half of adults have dangerously poor fitness. The proportion of children spending time in nature every day has fallen from 80 to 50 per cent in 20 years, and we see a growing fear of nature. While the evidence for nature's health benefits has become robust, the management of our most valuable natural areas has been severely neglected following major funding cuts.
Investment in physical activity and accessible nature delivers very strong returns.
See you under the large tree, with the sea as a backdrop.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Artistic freedom in turbulent times – from Katrineholm to Brussels
content.description: Freedom of expression, a fundamental part of democracy, has declined dramatically worldwide. How does this affect artistic freedom and policy for artists?
content.extendedDescription: Researchers at V-Dem-institutet at Göteborgs universitet conclude in a recently published report that freedom of expression, a fundamental part of democracy, has declined dramatically worldwide. We discuss with politicians, government agency representatives and opinion leaders how this affects artistic freedom, part of the freedom of expression protected by our constitution, at supranational, national and local levels. Among other issues, we address the European Commission's focus on protecting artistic freedom in the strategic framework ‘Culture Compass for Europe’ and discuss whether Swedish law also needs stronger protection for artistic freedom, taking the Museums Act as a starting point.

content.title: Multigenerational prevention – parenting support as a crime prevention measure
content.description: Children of parents involved in crime are at increased risk of becoming involved in crime themselves. For mothers facing multiple difficulties, a lack of trust in government agencies makes it harder to access support. How can relationship-based parenting support strengthen families and prevent vulnerability across generations?
content.extendedDescription:
Qrut meets mothers facing multiple difficulties: substance abuse, crime and exposure to violence, often combined with trauma, mental ill health and neurodevelopmental conditions. When trust in government agencies is absent, the path to support and change becomes long, sometimes almost non-existent.

We explore how civil society and government agencies can work together to make crime prevention interventions better targeted, more accessible and more lasting. Parenting support is not just care; it is also a crime prevention investment in the future. We share Qrut's unique working method and findings from current research on parenting support.

content.title: You will miss our nets when a crisis comes – household fishing and food preparedness
content.description: Everyone talks about the need for robust food preparedness, yet an inquiry is proposing a total ban on net fishing for household consumption. If we find ourselves in a serious crisis with food supplies under threat, every person with access to a boat and fishing gear will be vital.
content.extendedDescription:
Gotlands Husbehovsfiskeförening and Kullens Fiskareförening invite you to a discussion on the role of small-scale fishing in robust food preparedness in Sweden.
Coastal fishers know their waters; they know when and where to set their nets to catch fish. In a crisis, this is invaluable knowledge that society should make use of. Instead, fishing for household consumption faces a total ban, and coastal commercial fishing is struggling against industrial trawlers' high quotas and depleted fish stocks. Fish caught in our seas must become food for people, rather than being ground into fish and animal feed as they are today.
Come and listen to a discussion about the importance of small-scale fishing for our food supply, hear what politicians and public authorities think, ask questions and take the opportunity to learn more.
Welcome to our meeting point: fishing for household consumption – an important bearer of cultural traditions and essential to food supplies in a crisis.
content.subject: Food

content.title: Which food should be saved, and why – how do we reduce food waste sustainably?
content.description: In 2025, the EU adopted binding food waste targets. The focus often falls on reducing waste in retail and households. Yet every year, a hundred million meals are wasted in public-sector kitchens, along with up to 1 million tonnes of crops in fields. Given growing public health problems and overconsumption, which wasted food should we eat?
content.extendedDescription: Ätbart is a non-profit association that publishes annual food bank reports. In them, we highlight the fallacy in the idea that everything produced should be eaten to reduce food waste, and in its supposed environmental benefits. Reducing all waste indiscriminately through retail clearance sales or charitable donations does not necessarily lead to resource efficiency. Donations are an increasingly common way to reduce waste – but do they solve any problems, and what are their long-term consequences for social policy, the environment, the climate and public health? In this year's report, presented in a short lecture for event participants, Ätbart describes the problem of food losses in fields and serving waste in public-sector kitchens. The report gives examples of how the recently adopted legally binding food waste targets for large-scale catering can be achieved partly through redistribution as takeaway meals. It also presents good examples of partnerships between farms and local associations providing food support. A warm welcome!
content.subject: Food

content.title: Electric cars as an energy resource – how do we make the most of new technology to strengthen the electricity system?
content.description: Five million little cash cows travelling the roads and easing the load on the grid whenever they stop. It sounds a little too good to be true, but electric cars could soon become both financial successes and electricity system heroes. How do we make it happen?
content.extendedDescription: The technology is called vehicle-to-x and is about maximising the use of electric car batteries. If we can connect the batteries to the grid, they provide both power and system benefits. This helps the electricity system while generating income for car owners and accelerating electrification – a win-win-win. In this seminar, we join the sector's leading experts to get to the bottom of how to accelerate the technology. What is needed to make both charging infrastructure and cars ready for a large-scale introduction of ‘V2X’? And how can individuals and companies benefit? What is the actual scale of the potential?

content.description: Two-thirds of the world's refugees live in protracted displacement, entirely dependent on humanitarian aid. Can sustainable conditions for economic inclusion be created with shrinking aid budgets and more displaced people than ever?

content.title: Migration and development aid — how does KD want to shape policy after the next election?
content.description: The link between migration and development aid has gained political importance in Sweden and the EU. Aid is increasingly used to support migration policy objectives, raising questions about effectiveness, priorities and conflicting goals.
content.extendedDescription:
How do the parliamentary parties want to shape policy at the intersection of migration and development aid ahead of the next parliamentary term? In this discussion, Delmi and EBA invite representatives of the parties holding their party day in Almedalen to set out their priorities on an issue that has rapidly risen up the political agenda.

Drawing on current research and European experience, the discussion examines key choices: to what extent aid should be used for migration policy purposes, how different objectives should be balanced and which instruments should take priority. Topics include conditional aid, geographical priorities, deductions from aid budgets and possible departures from OECD-DAC rules.

The discussion aims to clarify the parties' positions and contribute to a more evidence-based debate on a policy area facing important choices.

content.title: Data between the committee and the construction site: Sweden's next productivity boost
content.description: With the right data linking political committees and construction sites, we can build a more productive Sweden. Political ambitions do not always reach those building society, and lessons from completed projects rarely reach decision-makers. How can AI close the gap and release billions?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's built-environment sector loses more than 100 billion kronor annually, with much determined in the gap between the committee and the construction site. This is the stage between political ambition and breaking ground, when tender documents, estimates and bids lock in project finances. Major decisions are made here, and major mistakes hidden. Political vision and technical reality speak different languages, and knowledge from completed projects rarely returns to decision-makers.

Brickanta and Verumatic have built two sides of the same bridge. Verumatic is an AI-driven platform analysing municipal political data and making it traceable. Brickanta is the agentic AI operating system that reads tender documents, learns from previous projects and gives built-environment professionals the conditions to build society.

This panel discusses how the data connects in practice: tracing political decisions into construction and bringing lessons from completed projects back to the committee.

content.title: European control and global technological capability – how do we find the cloud balance?
content.description: As cloud services, AI and data become critical infrastructure for society and business, Sweden and Europe face decisive strategic choices. The question is not whether to choose digital sovereignty or global innovation capacity, but how to combine them.

content.title: Children's rights as a compass in the climate crisis
content.description: The climate crisis is creating a growing gap between children's rights and the decisions shaping their future. A billion children already live at extremely high climate-related risk. This is a children's rights crisis, and many young people lack confidence in the future. How can children's perspectives guide the climate transition?
content.extendedDescription:
The climate crisis is not only an environmental crisis; it is a children's rights crisis. Around a billion children worldwide already live at extremely high climate-related risk, while many young people express declining confidence in the future. Climate change threatens children's rights to health, security, development and education: rights that the state is responsible for protecting under the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

Despite this, climate policy lacks a consistent children's rights perspective. Decisions are made with short time horizons, while today's children and future generations bear the consequences.

In this seminar, we explore the climate crisis as a children's rights crisis and ask: how can children's rights and future guide climate policy? What responsibility lies with politicians, businesses and adults, and what is needed for children's rights to guide practice rather than just rhetoric?

Welcome! Breakfast is served at 7:45.

content.title: From populism to national conservatism: the new right in Europe
content.description: Parties usually categorised as populist are now the largest or second-largest in several European countries. Are we witnessing the emergence of a national-conservative party family? How different are these parties? What happens to anti-establishment rhetoric when they enter government?
content.extendedDescription:
Support for so-called right-wing populist parties has increased throughout the 2000s. Today, parties such as Alternativ för Tyskland, Reform UK and France's Nationell samling are the largest or second-largest in almost every European democracy. Ten years after Brexit and Trump's first election victory, no one talks about “peak populism” anymore; instead, it seems obvious that these parties are here to stay.
How substantial are the similarities and differences between them? Is there an ideological consistency that makes it relevant to speak of a national-conservative party family? How does it differ from the old right? How have Trump and Putin influenced these parties' ideology? What happens to anti-establishment rhetoric when they enter government?

content.title: Sweden and Ukraine – how can universities keep functioning during acute crises?
content.description: Universities play an important role in peacetime, but what role do universities play during a societal crisis? Ukraine's universities have suffered under Russia's war of aggression, yet continue to operate. How can we support Ukraine and learn from their experiences?
content.extendedDescription: In peacetime, universities uphold democracy and culture, produce and disseminate knowledge about nature and society, advance health and quality of life, drive innovation, supply the labor market with educated workers, and much more. What becomes of the university's role when war or a profound societal crisis happens? Ukraine's universities are operating under extremely difficult conditions. The past winter has been especially difficult, and today the war has lasted longer than the Second World War. We will hear accounts of what the challenges of everyday life look like at Ukrainian universities. Many students and researchers are becoming soldiers, finances are strained, and conducting field research can be life-threatening. At the same time, Ukrainian universities are managing to continue their work. How can we offer Ukrainian researchers and universities partnerships that are mutually beneficial? Can we learn from the Ukrainian experience while offering concrete support here and now?

content.title: Low confidence in sharing health data – how does this affect new alliances in the healthcare ecosystem?
content.description: Swedish healthcare is at a crossroads. As care needs and staff shortages grow, citizens' expectations are changing. How can we secure an ecosystem that meets future needs and expectations?
content.extendedDescription: PwC and Apotek Hjärtat have investigated whether stakeholders beyond traditional healthcare providers could offer health-related services. All indications suggest the healthcare ecosystem could develop by giving other stakeholders new responsibilities. More than 1,500 citizens responded to a survey about their attitudes towards providers such as pharmacies, gyms and fitness centres and the roles these could play in the future ecosystem. An interesting finding is citizens' hesitation about sharing health data, a prerequisite for involving more stakeholders in the healthcare ecosystem. Several key stakeholders were also interviewed. Findings from the survey, interviews and document studies have been compiled in a report launched at this seminar during Almedalsveckan. We discuss the insights from this work with the aim of taking further steps in a direction.

content.title: We know what is coming – why are we not adapting better to climate change?
content.description: How do we make climate adaptation a natural part of planning and construction – rather than something we address when it is already too late?
content.extendedDescription:
Flooded homes. Closed schools. Businesses forced to shut their doors. These are not future scenarios – they are happening across Sweden right now.

Yet climate adaptation of the built environment is progressing too slowly. Not because we lack knowledge, but because responsibilities are poorly allocated, funding is insufficient and requirements are too weak.

The consequences are uninsurable properties and areas, disruption to essential services, and damage to infrastructure and buildings.

The next storm will not wait until we are ready.

During the seminar, Sweden Green Building Council (SGBC) highlights its report När stormen kommer, on accelerating climate adaptation of the built environment through a more reasonable allocation of responsibilities, smarter investments and tougher requirements. The seminar starts from the report's conclusions but focuses on the next step: what must the state, municipalities, public-sector clients and property owners do now, before the next cloudburst, storm or heatwave affects more people?
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: How do we future-proof large apartment housing estates?
content.description:
How do we create business models for a housing stock that is sustainable over the long term?
Sweden's apartment buildings need refurbishment, climate adaptation and stronger social conditions. This also raises a question: how can those contributing to safety and sustainable value creation share in neighbourhoods' increased value?
content.extendedDescription:
ShiftSweden's transition lab for future-proofing large apartment housing estates focuses on neighbourhoods built in the 1960s and 1970s that face major challenges concerning energy, social sustainability, finances, cultural heritage and long-term value creation. Taking the government's proposal for a new law on area-based cooperation as a starting point, we discuss the business models needed to make investment in safety, services, community, climate transition and technical refurbishment sustainable over the long term.

The event explores how property owners, businesses, civil society and public actors contributing to neighbourhood development can also share in the value they create. Hear research and discussion on translating social, environmental and economic sustainability into governance, financing and practical implementation, starting from existing buildings and place-based cooperation.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: How do we get housing construction moving – is building more houses the answer?
content.description: Construction is dominated by small apartments in major cities, while many people want to live in houses. Is it time for a new home ownership initiative, or more houses for rent? What political changes are needed to increase housing construction, and who should build?
content.extendedDescription:
How do we accelerate housing construction across the country, and what role can houses play? This panel discusses today's and tomorrow's challenges in getting housing construction moving. Why does production often get stuck on smaller apartments, what barriers block new projects, and how profitable is housebuilding? We discuss financing, land, planning processes and demand, and how a shift in construction could affect mobility, skills provision and the housing issue.

The discussion draws on observations from PwC's Emerging Trends 2026. The questions of which political changes are needed to increase housing construction, whether housebuilding can affect the housing shortage and who should build were highlighted by the panel as among the most important themes for 2026/2027.
content.subject: Construction

content.title: Taxes: an election weapon or a foundation for growth?
content.description: Taxes are crucial to the future of businesses and Sweden as a nation of entrepreneurs. But short-term thinking and bloc politics risk undermining long-term trust. Which tax issues matter most to businesses ahead of the election? And can politicians find common ground that creates stability?
content.extendedDescription:
Taxes affect everything from willingness to invest and entrepreneurship to changes of ownership and generational succession. But are politicians in tune with what Swedish businesses and their owners actually need? And how can Sweden create a more predictable tax policy that extends beyond a single parliamentary term?

The panel takes stock of Sweden's tax climate ahead of the election. Which reforms matter most? Where is the boundary between ideology and reality? And above all: is there a willingness to stop using taxes as a weapon in the election campaign?

In this panel debate during Almedalsveckan, PwC invites representatives of parliamentary parties and business organisations to discuss taxes, entrepreneurship and how Swedish tax policy can become a force for stability and growth.
content.subject: Business
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament and member of the Committee on Taxation

content.title: Finance in a new world order – resilience and adaptation in uncertain times
content.description: Geopolitical turmoil, the climate crisis and rapid technological development are shaping a new reality. How can the financial sector build resilience to uncertainty? How does a stable financial sector contribute to a more resilient society, and what leadership is needed when the future is difficult to read?
content.extendedDescription:
The global economy and geopolitical landscape are changing rapidly. Trade disputes, security tensions, the climate crisis and exponential technological development create new conditions, particularly for finance. As society's financial infrastructure, banks, insurers and asset managers play a crucial role in enabling the economy to function, businesses to invest and households to feel secure. The financial sector's resilience – its ability to withstand pressure, adapt and deliver – therefore concerns society as a whole.

The seminar begins with a macroeconomic outlook: where are we, and which scenarios should we prepare for? We then explore how the financial sector is affected, how it builds resilience and its role in society's ability to withstand disruption.

PwC brings together leading financial-sector voices to discuss changing conditions, strategic choices and the sector's growing societal responsibility.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: Doctors save lives – is our naivety playing into criminals' hands?
content.description: Criminal actors build their business on a vulnerable link: positions of trust. In the public sector and private business, people are lured or threatened into enabling different types of crime. How do we protect ourselves against criminal enablers, and how can we stop improper influence?
content.extendedDescription:
Journalist Lasse Wierup's book 'Maffiapakten' paints a frightening picture of how more criminal networks are targeting companies and public agencies in pursuit of easy money. Lawyers and doctors, as well as auditors, business leaders, bank staff and public employees, then become involved as enablers of organised crime. The results can include false certificates, improper decisions, information leaks, fraud and damage to both the economy and public trust.

Have we become too naive? For example, we often picture doctors wearing white coats and saving lives, rather than prescribing narcotics or issuing false medical certificates for payment or under pressure.

But what exactly is an enabler? Why does someone become one? How do we detect one? Above all, how can we protect ourselves, one another and our organisations against attempts to recruit enablers and exert improper influence?
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Coordinator for Welfare Crime, Improper Influence and Violent Extremism
Second Deputy Chair of Läkarförbundet and Chair of its Ethics Council

content.title: When geopolitics becomes code: cyberattacks against the Nordic region in a new security landscape
content.description: The Baltic Sea and Arctic have become central to great-power dynamics. Nordic energy production, submarine cables and digital infrastructure are strategic targets. State actors conduct grey-zone cyber operations: espionage, preparations for sabotage and influence campaigns. How do we build resilience?
content.extendedDescription:
Geopolitical tensions increasingly translate into concrete cyber activities against Nordic targets. State and state-linked actors use cyberattacks for pressure, intelligence gathering and signalling, often in the grey zone below the threshold of armed conflict. Reconnaissance, penetration testing and preparations for sabotage target critical infrastructure, while hybrid attacks such as DDoS attacks are combined with information manipulation and data leaks around political processes, elections and NATO milestones.

The seminar begins with a brief lecture by PwC's Cyber Threat Intelligence experts, outlining the Nordic region's place in today's security landscape, the geopolitical drivers of cyber operations and patterns of activity against Nordic targets.

The panel then addresses threats and trends, actors targeting the Nordic region, risk management informed by geopolitical analysis, cooperation between authorities and business, and other issues.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Climate risks and future crises – how can we prepare business and society?
content.description: Resilience is a business buzzword, but have climate risks made it into preparedness plans? Climate change can disable essential operations and critical services. How can boards and management prevent the effects of climate risks and build genuine resilience?
content.extendedDescription:
As climate change's impact becomes clearer, businesses face more and new challenges. Climate change increases the risk of extreme weather, supply-chain disruption and new requirements for businesses and other societal stakeholders. Yet many organisations remain inadequately equipped to manage climate risks within their routine governance and preparedness.

In this seminar, PwC brings together business and organisational representatives to discuss how boards and management can move from words to action. What is needed to integrate climate risks into strategy, risk management and decision-making? Who is responsible for strengthening resilience in an increasingly uncertain situation? And which reforms and priorities are needed to prepare business and society for future crises?

The audience will hear concrete perspectives on responsibility, preparedness and ways forward at a time when resilience has become crucial for competitiveness and society.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: How can we use AI safely and in ways that build trust?
content.description: AI is fundamentally changing both the public and private sectors – but how do we manage the risks as its use increases? How can we ensure that technological development goes hand in hand with security, responsibility and regulatory compliance?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is no longer a future issue for a select few, but a tool that can be useful to everyone, albeit in different ways. This makes AI a broad societal issue in which technological development, competitiveness, democracy and trust are closely connected. As more organisations integrate AI into their operations, it also becomes essential to understand what needs to be protected, regulated and monitored.

This seminar discusses two perspectives that increasingly need to be addressed together: technical security and regulatory requirements. How are organisations affected by new rules? What risks arise when AI models are used in sensitive processes or trained on large quantities of data? And how can management teams, experts and decision-makers strike the right balance between innovation, security and responsibility? AI solutions are also often used in legacy IT environments, creating additional security challenges.
The seminar will provide insights into how security work and regulations together shape the future use of AI.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Mandatory but flexible — how does the EU solidarity model affect Sweden?
content.description: The EU's new Pact on Migration and Asylum is based on a solidarity principle intended to distribute responsibility for receiving asylum seekers among member states. What does it mean in practice — and how might it affect Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
In spring 2024, the EU adopted a new Pact on Migration and Asylum. The pact includes the introduction of a mandatory but flexible solidarity mechanism. Its purpose is to redistribute responsibility away from member states under high migration pressure, mainly at the EU's external border, through mandatory relocations of asylum seekers, financial contributions or support in the form of resources and personnel, with countries choosing how to contribute. The mechanism replaces previous arrangements and is intended to create a more predictable division of responsibility within the EU. At the same time, it raises questions about how the balance between different forms of support will work in practice.

The discussion focuses particularly on what this means for Sweden. How might Sweden use the solidarity mechanism? What political and administrative choices arise, and how might Sweden's role in European cooperation be affected when the system starts to be applied?

content.title: Different needs, different messages – how pension information is changing
content.description: All pension savers are different, so why does the information look the same? We are now taking the next step towards more tailored pension information. What does that mean?
content.extendedDescription:
In June, minPension launches its first adaptation for younger pension savers. Others will also notice changes in how information is presented and what is highlighted.

But what does tailoring information to target groups mean in practice? What information matters at different life stages, and how do the needs of someone just starting work differ from those of someone about to draw their pension? The seminar discusses which questions savers actually want answered, what creates understanding rather than confusion, and the trade-offs required to make complex information more targeted and useful.

content.title: How do we increase voter turnout in socioeconomically disadvantaged neighbourhoods?
content.description: Differences in voter turnout between neighbourhoods are a growing democratic challenge in Sweden. Low participation in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas risks reinforcing inequality and reducing political equality. What measures can strengthen democratic participation?
content.extendedDescription:
Differences in voter turnout between neighbourhoods have increased over time and risk deepening existing socioeconomic divides. When people in some areas participate less, political equality and democratic representation suffer.

The discussion draws on a new knowledge review from Delmi, written by Karl-Oskar Lindgren, Professor of Political Science. The publication systematically reviews Swedish and international research on the causes of differences in democratic participation and measures shown to increase voter turnout in disadvantaged areas.

content.title: AI infrastructure for Swedish competitiveness — how can public authorities and businesses feel secure?
content.description: How do we build digital infrastructure in which both public authorities and businesses are secure and independent? How can we reduce vulnerability and create the conditions needed to strengthen Swedish innovation and sovereignty?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's future with AI is about infrastructure, energy and data centres as well as algorithms. Digital sovereignty is a prerequisite for building and operating effective, secure and energy-efficient data centres on our own terms. By controlling physical and digital infrastructure, from electricity supply and cooling to networks and storage, Sweden can strengthen innovation and retain its position as a high-tech, competitive country with scalable and sustainable AI capacity.

But do we really dare to make our future AI ecosystem dependent on infrastructure we do not control? Should Swedish energy policy and grid capacity be shaped around yesterday's IT needs when tomorrow's AI clusters require entirely different answers? And who actually sets the rules for where our most valuable data is stored — ourselves, or organisations far beyond our borders?

content.title: We want more than we think – why isn't climate commitment turning into action?
content.description: Swedes' commitment to the climate is greater than we think, but is systematically underestimated. This affects both behaviour and political decisions. What happens when decisions rest on a mistaken picture of public opinion, and how can we unlock the hidden scope for action?
content.extendedDescription:
Research and new Swedish data show that we systematically underestimate one another's willingness to contribute to the climate transition. In reality, there is broad support for both individual behavioural changes and political measures, but because we believe others are less committed than they are, we act accordingly.

This kind of social misperception affects not only individual behaviour but also which decisions are seen as politically possible. When decision-makers and citizens start from a mistaken view of public opinion, action may fail to happen despite existing support.

The seminar draws on the Peerpointing initiative's latest study, “Svenskarnas dolda klimatengagemang”, and focuses on the next step: putting this knowledge into practice.

content.title: Less administration, more trust: using resources efficiently to achieve a shared vision
content.description: How do we create real efficiency in knowledge-intensive organisations responsible for education, research and collaboration?
content.extendedDescription:
Many organisations want to reduce administration to free energy, time and resources for their core mission. Yet experience shows that savings alone rarely create real efficiency.
What is needed? Research and practice point to engaged leadership with a shared outlook, common working methods, clear roles and responsibilities, organisational trust and learning across boundaries. But the path also presents challenges: conflicting goals, us-and-them attitudes, limited shared understanding and turbulence at boundaries within organisations.
Using current examples, the seminar explores practical approaches combining data, dialogue, gradual change and respect for an organisation's own experience. The focus is on sustainable efficiency over time and reducing administration without losing quality or important support. Ultimately, it is about achieving common goals, realising a vision and contributing to social development.

content.title: New roles for business support organisations and investors – are they needed when the next unicorn is vibe-coded?
content.description: AI is reshaping the conditions for starting and running businesses. What makes a business idea sustainable over the long term when anyone can suddenly build services? How must Sweden's innovation system adapt to remain relevant as AI agents change the playing field?
content.extendedDescription:
The shift from AI assistant to AI agent creates entirely new demands on leadership, governance and business models, and on those supporting companies. Swedish SMEs lag substantially behind larger companies in AI adoption, creating gaps that will be difficult to close. Meanwhile, startups move from idea to product at record speed, with fewer employees and lower costs, using agentic AI and tools such as Claude Code. Two parallel realities emerge: those accelerating and building anew with AI as their engine, and those stopping at small incremental efficiencies.

How can Sweden's innovation system, including business support organisations and investors, support companies through this paradigm shift? What role should innovation stakeholders take, and what do companies need?

The seminar challenges the innovation system's self-image and discusses the roles business support organisations and investors need to take as the playing field changes in real time.

content.title: What actually is palliative care? On living life close to death
content.description: Palliative care often raises questions and fears. Many people immediately think of death. The focus is on living the life that remains to the fullest. Palliative care takes a holistic view of the person and aims to promote quality of life, reduce suffering and enable a meaningful life.
content.extendedDescription:
The event is a lecture in which we explain palliative care simply and clearly. We see value in clarifying what palliative care is and what it involves, as misunderstandings currently create fear. We want to show how palliative care supports life at its most fragile and is not about giving up. Reports show that access to palliative care in Sweden is unequal and that unclear perceptions and fears may be part of the explanation.
The lecture draws on research and relates to Socialstyrelsen's updated definitions and guidelines. Palliative care is provided for conditions that may lead to death within days, months or years, and therefore needs to be integrated into other healthcare and social care.
There is a great need for knowledge. We hope the lecture will dispel myths, spark curiosity and provide an understanding of what palliative care is and why it concerns us all.

content.title: Beyond the crisis headlines: how is liberalism really doing?
content.description: 30 years ago, liberalism's future looked bright. Then came declining confidence in liberal democracy and growing dissatisfaction with globalisation, capitalism and individualism. What happened? Did liberalism lose its appeal when liberal democracy triumphed?
content.extendedDescription:
Thirty years ago, liberalism's future looked bright. When the Berlin Wall fell, many believed a freer, more peaceful and richer world lay ahead. What followed during the first quarter of the twenty-first century was democratic decline, falling confidence in liberal democracy and new conflicts both within and between countries. Dissatisfaction with globalisation, capitalism and individualism is growing among Western populations. While it has been a difficult quarter-century for liberal parties, much has happened in the development of liberal ideas.

What happened? Did liberalism as an ideology lose its appeal when liberal democracy triumphed? Do liberal parties have answers to today's political questions? Does an era of postliberalism await, or is liberalism's self-confidence lower than it should be?

content.title: Policy for mental health: what does it mean?
content.description: Mental ill-health is one of Sweden's greatest public health challenges. One in three people is affected, and everyone knows someone. The disease burden and societal costs are enormous, yet in practice healthcare budgets are not increasing and care is unequal. We need a policy for mental health, but what does that mean?
content.extendedDescription:
Partnerskap för psykisk hälsa welcomes you to a lively discussion between regional politicians from different parties about raising the priority of efforts to address mental ill-health, creating a more coordinated, person-centred care pathway, and improving working conditions and the skills supply.

We cannot afford either the economic costs or the human suffering caused by mental ill-health. Real change requires long-term political responsibility and resource allocation that prioritises mental health. The National Strategy for Mental Health and Suicide Prevention is a start, but what policies are needed for real change in the regions?

In this seminar, Partnerskap för psykisk hälsa focuses on how we can contribute to long-term mental health policy: policy that makes a real difference.

content.title: The economic outlook in 2026: recovery with risks – what lies ahead for Sweden and the world?
content.description: What does the economic outlook look like in 2026? How do geopolitical conflicts, inflation, interest rates and the labour market affect economic development, and what does this mean for businesses, households and decision-makers?
content.extendedDescription: Dagens industri and +Pro invite you to a trend overview with Anna Ekelund, News Editor at Dagens industri. After several years of recession, signs of recovery are emerging in Sweden and globally, but progress is fragile and risks are numerous. The conflict in the Middle East and rising energy prices have dampened growth and increased inflationary pressure, while Sweden's economy benefits from strong public finances and competitive businesses. Household consumption drives the recovery, but unemployment remains high and differences between groups are growing. GDP growth forecasts range from 2 to 3 per cent, but uncertainty is substantial and the future depends on geopolitics, energy prices and global trade. We discuss the key trends, risks and opportunities.

Members of ST inom Polisen are also often the people you meet when you contact the police.

content.title: Visby's water shortage – what are we doing now, and how do we solve it in the long term?
content.description: Visby's water supply has long faced capacity shortages and, in recent years, quality deviations too. Several measures are now being implemented at existing facilities to strengthen supplies over the coming years. In the longer term, Visby's water supply needs further reinforcement.
content.extendedDescription:
Meeting the challenges while laying the foundations for a sustainable future water supply requires both short- and long-term measures:
1. Short-term measures: renovating and strengthening pipelines, waterworks and reservoirs, and connecting to Södra Gotlands avsaltningsverk.

content.title: An energy system that lasts: how do we secure Sweden's future energy supply?
content.description: Energy needs are growing, and secure, reliable, reasonably priced energy is crucial to society, businesses and people. Geopolitical uncertainty strains the system but may also accelerate transition. How do we jointly shape sustainable energy infrastructure for Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
Energy supply is central to the global transition. Delivering it while meeting rapidly rising energy demand requires new forms of cooperation between business and society. We begin by examining barriers affecting energy availability, including technology, regulations, investment and the constantly changing international situation. How do we balance growing electrification with capacity shortages, challenging costs, a pressing maintenance backlog and stronger robustness requirements that drive major investment needs?

We also discuss how new technology and partnerships between society and businesses can secure a stable, safe and affordable energy supply. How can new perspectives support novel energy storage solutions and alternative raw materials that strengthen the system over time?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Can AI strengthen democracy and solve societal problems — for real?
content.description: Can AI be used to lower barriers to democratic participation, increase young people's voter turnout and build trust in society's institutions? How do we move from technology and vision to solving major societal challenges in areas such as climate, health, education, inclusion and humanitarian work?
content.extendedDescription:
How do we take AI from technology and vision to real positive impact in areas such as democracy, climate, health, education, inclusion and humanitarian work?

Can we use AI to strengthen democracy, increase participation and build trust in society's institutions? Drawing, among other things, on our hackathon at Järvaveckan — based on the question of how to motivate more young people to vote in the coming election — we discuss how AI can move from idea to real societal benefit.

The panel brings together different perspectives — technology, ethics, law and societal development — to discuss how we can accelerate both AI adoption and benefits to society. AI is one of the most powerful technologies of our time, but its real value is determined by how, and for what, it is used.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Following the money – what is banks' role in combating welfare crime?
content.description: The criminal economy turns over SEK 352 billion a year, and welfare crime is a growing part of it. Banks have unique insight into transactions, patterns and anomalies that can signal abuse of welfare systems early. What is banks' role in combating welfare crime?
content.extendedDescription:
Banks' role in combating welfare crime involves stopping the flows of the criminal economy. Their central position in the financial system allows banks to detect unusual transaction patterns, suspicious arrangements and structures linked to systematic abuse of welfare systems early – things that might otherwise remain invisible to individual public agencies.

However, effective work requires more than traditional regulatory compliance. As crime becomes more sophisticated, banks' role in prevention and detection grows. Realising this potential requires closer cooperation with the public sector, clear structures for information sharing and a shared understanding of how welfare crime is organised and financed. Technology, data analysis and shared risk assessments become central tools.

The panel discussion examines banks' societal role, obstacles in current regulations and how stronger cooperation can protect welfare systems.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: How do municipalities address national digitalisation initiatives in light of local needs?
content.description: Fewer people must deliver welfare services to more people, and digitalisation is seen as an important way forward. Municipal conditions vary, while national stakeholders offer shared solutions. How are national and local initiatives balanced in practice, and what effects are achieved?
content.extendedDescription:
With an ageing population and fewer working-age people, Sweden's municipalities and welfare services face major challenges. Digitalisation is often presented as the solution, with scalable technologies that can streamline processes and create value through new ways of working. National stakeholders such as the government, DIGG and SKR support municipalities with shared frameworks and digital solutions, but how do municipalities balance national initiatives with local needs and priorities?

The seminar starts from a master's thesis by a PwC employee who researched implementation of national digitalisation initiatives at municipal level in spring 2026. Based on in-depth interviews with representatives of 20 municipalities, the study offers a unique insight into conditions across the country. The panel brings together SKR, municipal and academic representatives to discuss the interaction between national and local digitalisation work in improving and developing welfare services.

content.title: When AI becomes a colleague: who does what, and who is responsible?
content.description: AI has moved from a passive tool to an actor making decisions and driving workflows. This places entirely new demands on responsibility, leadership and employees' interaction with technology. How do we prepare organisations for this change, and who is responsible?
content.extendedDescription:
This panel starts from the rapid development of agentic AI systems that no longer merely support people, but can independently perform and coordinate work. As AI becomes a colleague, the allocation of tasks, responsibilities and decision-making authority changes.

We discuss redesigning work when people and AI operate side by side. Which tasks should AI perform, and which require human judgement? Who is responsible when decisions emerge from human–machine interaction? We address leadership, skills and ethics, and whether organisations can afford to delay taking these choices seriously.
We also present insights from this year's AI Jobs Barometer on AI's effects on jobs, skills requirements and the allocation of responsibility in the labour market.

content.title: Do older people in Sweden have weaker legal protection than animals, and why do we not talk more about it?
content.description: For almost 150 years, weekly magazines have been a natural part of everyday life. They reach a large and often overlooked audience: women in later middle age. How do you deliver public-interest journalism where the audience already is, but is rarely taken seriously?
content.extendedDescription:
For almost 150 years, the weekly magazines Allers, Allas, Hemmets Veckotidning and Året Runt have been a natural part of everyday life. Behind the short stories, recipes and crosswords, something more is happening. We use the power of lifestyle journalism to highlight issues that truly matter, and sometimes shake things up. Our widely discussed investigation Hemtjänsthaveriet revealed an uncomfortable truth: in practice, older people in Sweden have weaker legal protection than animals. How did this happen, and why do we allow it to continue?
Join a conversation about journalism that engages, challenges and makes an impact. How do you steward a cultural heritage dating from the nineteenth century while making it relevant in a digital age?
Meet editor-in-chief Åsa Liliegren and editor Maria Torshall for a conversation about the power of taking your audience seriously, combining warmth with courage, and why this kind of journalism can be crucial to driving change.

content.title: Does international law have a future?
content.description: Wars, conflicts and global power shifts challenge the foundations of the international legal system. Is international law still relevant, or has it already outlived its role as an international framework for justice and accountability?
content.extendedDescription:
When great powers act outside shared rules, the relevance of international law is questioned, while others argue that it remains an important and resilient foundation for international cooperation. International law rests on states' consent and compliance, making its strength dependent on political will. When states leave agreements such as the Ottawa Convention or breach principles such as non-intervention, they risk eroding norms and legitimising similar behaviour.

This seminar discusses the future of international law at a time when power and norms frequently collide. Has international law weakened, transformed or lost its significance?

The seminar forms part of Folk och Försvar's arena in Almedalen, a meeting place for dialogue, knowledge exchange and new perspectives on Sweden's security. Stakeholders from across society come together to contribute to a safe, free and democratic Sweden.

content.title: Between facts and political opinion
content.description: A knowledge gap between research and politics can affect the prospects for sustainable, legally sound political decisions over the long term. How can research have greater impact in public debate, and what can actually be done with research findings?
content.extendedDescription:

The two-hour discussion is divided into three parts, with plenty of time for questions and networking between them. This second discussion concerns the roles of researchers, investigators, experts and political officials in policy and implementation, how research can have greater impact in debate and what may be done with research findings.

content.title: Cultural heritage under attack!
content.description: Anundshög, one of our most iconic Viking Age archaeological sites, has been looted over the past year. This is not an isolated incident, but a growing national problem. Museums play an important role in sharing knowledge, but who is responsible for protection and preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
Västerås museer, Gotlands Museum and many other museums meet an engaged and concerned public wanting to know what is being done to protect our shared cultural heritage.
At a time when societal preparedness is high on the agenda, protecting our shared cultural heritage has gained renewed relevance, particularly in the event of war. Ensuring that it is not damaged in peacetime should be at least as important. Quiet, systematic destruction of cultural heritage is taking place. Metal detector use is particularly serious: in practice, national coordination is lacking and responsibility for supervision is unclear. The lack of current research and investigation into heritage crime is striking. We call for:
• A national strategy and coordination against heritage crime to address ongoing looting, particularly illegal metal detecting.
• More resources for supervision, education and research into heritage crime.
content.subject: Culture

content.title: How can Sweden attract more and larger industrial investments?
content.description: Ireland's systematic efforts have made it a global pharmaceutical powerhouse. Can Sweden copy the recipe and attract more cash?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has a strong identity as an industrial nation and has long been an attractive location for investment in production. But the trend is declining – both the number and the share of foreign investments in Swedish industry are shrinking.

The dwindling number of industrial investments in Sweden and the EU is a problem with major risks as the renewal of know-how and related services contracts. To meet increasingly fierce global competition, industry must develop and grow. Other countries are doing better. What can Sweden do to become more attractive to investment? Welcome to an engaging seminar with an international outlook and concrete examples of what is needed!

content.title: From vulnerability to strength — a new situation for Swedish cybersecurity
content.description: What political, technical and procurement decisions are needed to move from vulnerability to operational strength in Swedish cybersecurity and total defence?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's cybersecurity is determined not only by technical capacity or political ambitions, but to a large extent by the requirements actually set when the public sector procures digital infrastructure, systems and security solutions.

European analyses show that the public sector today depends heavily on a few large, often non-European suppliers, particularly in digital infrastructure. The issue is therefore not merely cost, but how established requirements, procurement patterns and market structures affect which solutions are sought and selected.

Against this background, the seminar focuses on procurement as a strategic tool for strengthening cybersecurity, innovation and resilience — if the right requirements are set. Drawing on perspectives from business and the public sector, we discuss how Sweden can use procurement to reduce vulnerable dependencies, strengthen domestic and European markets and raise operational security.

content.title: Is evidence still relevant in politics?
content.description: What obstacles, opportunities and concrete ways forward do we see for achieving more evidence-based political decision-making? And is it always desirable?
content.extendedDescription:
Over an afternoon (14.00-16.00), we will examine the concept of evidence in relation to decision-making, governance and implementation in Swedish politics. The two-hour discussion is divided into three parts, with plenty of time for questions and networking between them. The aim is a nuanced dialogue about how more knowledge-driven decision-making can contribute to more precisely targeted, legally sound and effective policy interventions.

In this third discussion, politics and research meet to examine evidence's role in practice. Drawing on concrete experiences in education policy, we discuss where knowledge has an impact and where it is pushed aside. A broader discussion about evidence aiming to identify how we can make better use of everything we already know.

14.00-14.30 Does Swedish politics need more evidence?
14.40-15.10 Between facts and political opinion

content.title: 89% want stronger climate policy – what could the measures look like?
content.description: A majority of the world's population (89%) wants stronger climate action. Yet creative ideas and smart measures are conspicuously absent. Klimatklubben wants to change that!
content.extendedDescription:
According to a global study, a majority of the world's population wants stronger climate action.

Wanting strong climate policy is more common than watching Mello or being an adult with a driving licence in Sweden. Yet both climate issues and measures are conspicuously absent from the debate.
The non-profit organisation Klimatklubben wants to change that.

In a talk show hosted by Klimatklubben co-founders Maria Soxbo and Emma Sundh, a succession of guests will brainstorm creative, smart measures that reduce emissions and/or support biodiversity. In short: make a real difference.
The goal? A bank of ideas for political parties to draw on and a wealth of measures for citizens to demand.

content.title: The skills gap is growing – how can we secure the next generation of engineers?
content.description:
How can we ensure Sweden meets the growing need for engineering skills to address societal challenges:
The green transition
Defence capability
Industrial competitiveness
Jobs and welfare
content.extendedDescription:
Panel debate led by the Editor-in-Chief of Ny Teknik.
Demand for engineering skills in STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) is rising rapidly as AI, digitalisation, advanced industry, electrification and cybersecurity reshape business. Meanwhile, national assessments show current educational capacity is insufficient. Just over 80,000 people currently study STEM at higher education level in Sweden, and the government aims to increase this to at least 90,000 by 2035.
Sweden thus faces a decisive technological shift in which skills requirements are changing faster than education, continuing training and the ability to attract students can keep up. Too few choose technical programmes relative to growing needs, while global competition for talent intensifies. The result is a growing gap between education and labour market needs, with direct consequences for Sweden's innovative strength, investment and long-term competitiveness.
