content.title: Who can influence cancer care – and on what terms?
content.description: Patient involvement is central to developing future cancer care. But whose experiences inform that development, and whose risk being absent? How can we create forms of participation that reach more people and better reflect the patient population?
content.extendedDescription:
Patient and family involvement is central to developing future cancer care. Yet experience and research show that opportunities to influence care vary. Some groups remain underrepresented in settings where care is shaped and developed.

This matters. Young adults are a small group in cancer care, but their life circumstances often differ from those of both younger children and older adults. When young people's experiences are absent, important needs also risk going unmet.

Join an inspiring seminar exploring how patient involvement can work in practice! What is needed for more people to have a say? How can we ensure patients' perspectives have an impact? And what can healthcare, research and other stakeholders gain from more voices being heard?

Concrete examples from young adults affected by cancer, healthcare, research and national development work highlight methods, lessons and opportunities for more representative patient involvement.

Breakfast will be served!

content.title: Protected sites: national security and uncertainty
content.description: How do we create narratives about security and uncertainty in dialogue with others? What influence do storytelling and stories have on strategic and military decisions?
content.extendedDescription:
This year, a green military accommodation tent will stand on Almedalen's shore. Inside, we will perform a play connecting Gotland's past and present as a strategically important military location with fears and concerns about Gotland's and Sweden's future security.
Two signals intelligence operators are working at a temporary mobile reconnaissance station. Suddenly, one notices an anomaly on the screen. What are they seeing? And what should they do about it? Perhaps everything is about to change.
A play by Julia Hackman
Cast: Anton Cöster and Evelina Benedicks

The performance lasts 50 minutes and is staged in the tent four times a day: at 10:30, 12:45, 14:30 and 16:00. Between performances, the tent is open for visitors to step inside. Admission is free, but places are limited. To secure a place, register in advance using the web link below.

In cooperation with Kulturföreningen Roxy.

content.title: No peace without justice — what can we do about impunity for international crimes in Ukraine?
content.description: Russia's invasion of Ukraine constitutes a serious violation of international law. At the same time, civilians are subjected to indiscriminate attacks. There are also extensive reports of war crimes committed by Russian forces, including torture of prisoners of war, sexual violence against civilians and the deportation of children.
content.extendedDescription:
Join a seminar offering an up-to-date overview of efforts to combat impunity for international crimes in Ukraine: Who has the mandate to investigate war crimes and bring perpetrators to justice? How can evidence be secured in a way that stands up in court? Why is a special tribunal for the crime of aggression needed? And what is being done to ensure compensation for those affected?

During the seminar, we highlight how individuals, civil society organisations and states can contribute to justice. Aggression must not pay. International crimes must not go unpunished. And the harm caused must be recognised and compensated.

Together, we can counter impunity and work towards accountability for Ukraine — because without justice, there is no lasting peace.
content.subject: International affairs
speakerTitles: EU Special Representative for Human Rights

content.title: The Fehmarn Belt tunnel is changing the Nordic region – is Sweden ready?
content.description: How can we ensure a functioning transport network as pressure increases? When the Fehmarn Belt tunnel between Denmark and Germany opens, Sweden will gain a faster, more direct connection to the continent.
content.extendedDescription:
This strengthens Nordic competitiveness and our opportunities to connect more closely with Europe.
At the same time, pressure on our own transport links is increasing, with bottlenecks on routes including Skåne–Själland and Oslo–Göteborg. Öresundsbron and the Oslo–Göteborg connection are already heavily used. So how can we ensure that the system holds up, including during crises and disruptions?

Join a panel discussion on strengthening both capacity and preparedness in our transport networks, and how cross-border cooperation can provide more robust solutions for the future.

We discuss:
• Where are the local bottlenecks or “missing links” in the transport network?
• What do the Swedish regions concerned need to meet future mobility needs?
• How can we on the Swedish side meet increased capacity requirements in the connections between Sweden and Denmark, and between Sweden and Norway?
• How can Nordic cooperation help create sustainable and resilient solutions?

content.title: Strategic or naive – how should Sweden navigate defence and conflict prevention?
content.description: As global security becomes unstable, political priorities favour defence over aid and diplomacy. Meanwhile, humanitarian needs are exploding amid more conflicts, a rapidly worsening climate crisis and displacement. What does security actually mean, and how can we build it?
content.extendedDescription:
Aid is declining when humanitarian needs have never been greater. Military spending is rising instead. Security is increasingly defined in terms of defence, while research shows that long-term stability is built through investment in democracy, human rights and conflict prevention. What role do Sweden's aid and foreign policies play in today's security situation? Questions include:
• Is prioritising prevention politically possible without appearing naive in today's world?
• What is the cost of focusing solely on defence and reducing investment in preventing conflicts, pandemics and climate-related disasters?
• How should we shape future security policy, diplomacy and aid as the global map of power changes?
• What role should Sweden take?
Join an in-depth discussion of what Swedish policy needs to genuinely contribute to a safer, more stable world.

content.title: Future of Everything: Sweden's and Europe's place in an AI-dominated world
content.description: AI is changing the foundations of business, culture, democracy and competitiveness. The question is not whether change is coming, but what happens to Sweden and Europe when it does. What choices must we make now to avoid becoming passengers in a future determined by others?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is set to redefine what drives growth, what counts as human creativity, how Europe defends its autonomy and what intelligence means at all. Future of Everything comprises four short stage discussions approaching these questions from different perspectives.

Future of Business: What is needed for Sweden to keep producing world-class companies as AI reshapes value chains?

Future of Europe: What will the European AI stack look like in five years, and what does autonomy mean in practice?

Future of Creativity: What happens to art, copyright and the creative professions when machines become co-creators?

Future of Everything: What will remain of us as humans when machines take over more and more of what previously defined us?
content.subject: Business

content.title: How do we accelerate the circular transition? Business solutions for a sustainable future
content.description: Sweden has ambitious climate and environmental goals. National targets and EU requirements are driving a green transition in which waste is increasingly seen as a resource. Meanwhile, business is now being given greater responsibility for efficient recycling and circular material flows.
content.extendedDescription:
The government has recently reformed waste legislation to create better conditions for recycling. But legislation on paper is one thing; functioning systems in practice are another. How does this affect companies' opportunities to invest and develop new circular solutions? And which parts of the regulatory framework need further simplification to achieve ambitious climate and environmental goals?

Join a seminar presenting concrete examples of circular solutions that work in practice. We discuss opportunities and ways to strengthen cooperation throughout the value chain, and address challenges still slowing the transition.

What is needed here and now to remove further barriers, create functioning markets for recycled materials and meet Sweden's commitments? Meet representatives of politics, public agencies and business for a discussion about a long-term framework and how to achieve a circular economy that delivers both climate benefits and competitiveness.
content.subject: Sustainability
speakerTitles: feedstock trader & analyst in HVO value chain

content.title: Landfills and detoxification in a circular economy – managing society's most difficult waste
content.description: Not all waste can be recycled. In a circular economy, some flows are complex, requiring long-term solutions and making detoxification crucial. How has the waste sector developed, and what exactly is a landfill – and why is it still needed?
content.extendedDescription:
Society's difficult waste requires a comprehensive approach, with its management crucial both to the climate transition and to access to important resources. How can sorting and quality-assured flows be prerequisites for effective material recycling, and why should not all waste be returned to the cycle?

Join a seminar in which we work across the value chain to highlight both opportunities and challenges in today's modern waste management, from waste to resource.

What is needed here and now to remove obstacles, create functioning markets for recycled materials and achieve Sweden's climate and environmental targets? Meet politicians, authorities and businesses for a discussion on the need for long-term conditions, efficient permitting processes and greater visibility for the enormous infrastructure required to handle difficult waste in a robust, resource-efficient waste system that benefits the climate.

content.title: To the Swedish mountains by fossil-free coach
content.description: Can coaches become an attractive complement to trains for climate-smart travel to the Swedish mountains? Industry players are challenging fossil fuels to a snowball fight.
content.extendedDescription:
The transition towards fossil-free operations is under way throughout the transport chain, and interest in climate-smart travel is strong. Interest in domestic holidays is also growing, and trains already offer many people a good alternative to taking the car. Yet around 9 out of 10 families drive to the Swedish mountains. Perhaps this is unsurprising: every family going on a skiing holiday knows the challenge of fitting skis, ski boots and everything else into the roof box and boot, so taking the train can feel like too great a logistical challenge. A modern, climate-smart coach can offer an appealing alternative for travelling almost door to door!

At this seminar, representatives from throughout the chain describe today's situation and future opportunities for fossil-free, sustainable coach travel to the Swedish mountains. Who knows: perhaps even Stig-Helmer Olsson will turn up to pre-book a coach trip and accommodation in the annexe?

content.title: The world's best healthcare system – why is it developing in sparsely populated areas?
content.description: In inland Västerbotten, there is one of the world's best primary healthcare systems, recognised by organisations including the WHO. Since 2025, a national assignment has focused on knowledge development, research and innovation, working with the rest of Sweden to take the next step towards even better care.
content.extendedDescription: Care models and smart working methods centred on individuals show that good, equitable care can be provided around the clock even in sparsely populated areas, despite long distances and demographic changes that leave fewer people to meet an ageing population's needs. Conditions for health and care in sparsely populated areas differ in many ways from those in urban settings. Long distances mean more care must be provided locally, primary care staff need both broad and specialised expertise, and regions, municipalities and residents must cooperate closely. Rapid technological development and access to data create new opportunities but also place greater demands on organisation, working methods and skills. How can we ensure that people, organisations and systems are equipped for this transition, so technology supports rather than complicates equitable, locally accessible care in rural and sparsely populated areas throughout Sweden?

content.title: The Stockholm of the future – strategies for even more urban life, experiences and innovation
content.description: Long-term urban development requires both courage and new thinking, especially in changing times. What opportunities are offered by existing built structures and the blue-green assets that characterise Stockholm? And how can urban planning continue to drive the realisation of visions?
content.extendedDescription:
Stockholm has always been a city of development and change. Over the past 25 years, it has grown by 250 000 new residents in 100 000 new homes, with new workplaces, public services, attractive public spaces and infrastructure, particularly through expanded public transport. All of this is rooted in long-term plans spanning many decades, which the city and everyone involved have been good at bringing to life.

What could Stockholm look like in the 2060s – what opportunities does our future offer? Work is currently under way to shape that future in a new comprehensive plan. Which of today's known conditions are given space alongside what is still unknown and unplanned? And how do we use urban development in our everyday lives to create an even more attractive city to live in?

Meet representatives from the city and the sector who share their vision of the future. They also show how the city is developing today through urban development that adds value, making Stockholm an even better city for everyone.

content.title: Who decides over the landscape during the energy transition?
content.description: The energy transition must happen, and it needs space. Invisible harmful emissions are replaced by energy infrastructure visible in landscapes where people live and work. Municipalities and regions increasingly need to demonstrate local leadership, authority and the ability to make courageous decisions.
content.extendedDescription:
Energikontoren Sverige, together with #Krafttag i Väst – ElSA, invites you to this seminar, drawing on current research on regional energy planning and highlighting regions' role in managing conflicts between climate, industry, natural values and local acceptance. We also focus on municipalities' crucial role, where their planning monopoly and local decision-making powers must translate into actions that drive the transition.
Using examples from Dalarna, Energikontoret i Östergötland's energy planning work, the SpeedLocal research project on social acceptance and Fyrbodals kommunalförbund's politically adopted direction, we discuss how strategic planning can become concrete municipal action, and what is needed to dare to prioritise conflicting interests.
The discussion is moderated by Tomas Kåberger, Chair of Energikontoren Sverige.
The seminar offers:
• Insights, perspectives and examples of municipalities' role as enablers of energy expansion.

content.title: Climate adaptation and digital services – AI and data-driven decisions for a more resilient society
content.description: As extreme weather such as flooding, storms and drought increases, banks, insurers and property owners face growing climate risks. Digital solutions, data-driven decisions and AI can help predict, quantify and reduce risks, both physically and financially.
content.extendedDescription:
In a changing climate, we see more frequent and intense extreme weather events, such as torrential rain, flooding and wildfires, as well as long-term changes such as extended dry periods and rising sea levels. This creates growing climate risks for banks, insurers and property owners, at both asset and portfolio level.
At the same time, digital solutions, data analysis and AI create new opportunities to understand, anticipate and manage these risks. Combining data, climate scenarios and analysis can reveal, quantify and in some cases prevent risks, both physically and financially.
The discussion brings together perspectives on managing climate risks in a changing climate. It focuses on how data, experience and digital tools can support better-informed decisions and greater preparedness in banking, insurance and property, as well as municipal planning.

content.title: Endless possibilities for future infrastructure – how can the sector step up?
content.description: Sweden has a great need for resilient infrastructure. It needs to be built promptly, sustainably and cost-effectively. If technology, methods and expertise are available, how can the sector cooperate to deliver value faster? Could openness, considered risk-taking and courage be the answer?
content.extendedDescription:
There are major opportunities to build infrastructure in modern ways. Technology has advanced rapidly, new methods are available and with them comes the opportunity to build infrastructure more cheaply, quickly and resiliently. Yet despite rapid technological development, our sector has not managed to implement it at the pace society needs. We have a chance to catch up, eliminate the maintenance backlog, increase preparedness and build a sustainable society. Today, outdated regulations and a lack of broad agreements stand in the way. We risk locking ourselves into old technology. Collaboration and an innovative approach now offer an opportunity to get more infrastructure for the money. So what do we need to do?
In this discussion, decision-makers from public agencies and business meet to consider how we can deliver future infrastructure sooner.

content.title: From fossil fuels to the future: aviation's transition
content.description: Can we keep flying while reducing our climate impact? And how do geopolitical crises affect the transition?
content.extendedDescription:
What does it really take to make air travel sustainable, and what role do we ourselves play in that transition? Biofuels are often presented as a solution for long-haul flights, but how do we ensure that raw materials such as forestry and slaughterhouse waste are used without creating new problems? How do we ensure a sustainable supply chain behind the fuel?

Meanwhile, many point to the potential of electric aviation. But if electric motor technology already exists, are batteries, infrastructure or investment the real challenge?

And another important question: how do we actually view flying in the future? If flying is already accessible to relatively few people, what does making it more sustainable mean? Is it only about new technology, or also about travelling differently, less often and more consciously?

Join a conversation about fuel, technology and responsibility in aviation's transition between Elna Heimdal Nilsson, Professor of Aeronautical Sciences at Lunds universitet, and Thomas Frostberg, innovation and business journalist.

content.title: How do we create national climate infrastructure for Swedish cities and climate initiatives?

The event takes the form of a discussion with short contributions from organisations working on climate-neutral cities, the construction sector's transition, roadmaps and digital climate data. It focuses on whether shared data, methods and tools can reduce duplication, improve comparability, provide better decision support for urban development and procurement, and contribute to climate-neutral cities. content.title: How to design capacity charges that work
content.description: Capacity charges are intended to shift electricity use away from periods of heavy grid load, freeing up capacity and keeping costs down. But the current model is now being challenged politically. How can charges be designed to be effective, fair and understandable for customers?
content.extendedDescription:
Capacity charges are intended to shift electricity use away from periods when the grid is heavily loaded. The aim is to enable greater electrification without extensive grid expansion, thereby lowering the total cost for electricity customers. During the spring, the current design of the charges has been heavily criticised in public debate. Energy Minister Ebba Busch has therefore tasked Energimarknadsinspektionen with developing a new proposal.
Two Energiforsk projects have analysed how capacity tariffs can be designed. UniFlex has developed an hourly capacity charge based on forecasts, charged only when expected grid load is high. At other times the charge is zero, so it does not, for example, deter electric vehicle charging when electricity prices are low.
K-flex starts from the growing importance of demand flexibility and energy storage. Enabling customers to help limit the need for grid expansion requires economic incentives that are clear in both time and location, and tools to counter local overload.

content.title: Construction boom, concrete shortage and preparedness – new conditions for material supply
content.description: Construction faces material shortages and vulnerable supply chains, while concrete is increasingly prioritised for total defence expansion and critical infrastructure. Climate, security and availability must be weighed against each other. How can we build when concrete supply is no longer assured?
content.extendedDescription:
A changing world, with security concerns, vulnerable supply chains and new wartime preparedness requirements, fundamentally affects construction planning and delivery. Meanwhile, construction and property must transition to lower climate impacts and more efficient resource use. Concrete, long taken for granted in infrastructure and essential buildings, has therefore become a strategic resource requiring trade-offs between availability, climate threats and wartime preparedness.
When material availability can no longer be assumed, perspectives must broaden. Circular material flows, reuse, new structural principles, alternative construction methods and hybrid solutions can contribute to both total defence and climate benefits, but bring new risks and trade-offs.
This open discussion explores how construction can strengthen resilience through better analysis, early choices and interdisciplinary collaboration between clients, industry, authorities and technical consultants.

content.description: Industry is held back by growing skills shortages while education fails to match needs. How do we secure skills provision? This is central to competitiveness and regional development but requires new collaboration models between education and working life.
content.extendedDescription:
What challenges and needs does Swedish industry face today?
To help address them, we are creating Industrins tekniska lärcentrum (ITLC) together with partners.

Industrial skills shortages are a growing societal challenge affecting growth, innovation and the green transition. Meanwhile, a gap remains between education and labour market needs.
The seminar explores how to strengthen practical knowledge, make industry more attractive through modern, representative environments and create more APL and LIA work-based learning placements. It focuses on solutions, barriers and new collaboration models for sustainable skills provision.

content.title: What can we learn from Ukraine for our own resilience and societal development?
content.description: During the ongoing war, Ukraine has demonstrated an impressive ability to maintain essential services, rebuild what has been destroyed and develop new innovations. Its experiences cover both protecting essential infrastructure and new material flows. What can we learn from its agility?
content.extendedDescription:
How do our cities function when the power fails, water runs out and roads are clogged with abandoned cars? Sweden can learn important lessons from Ukraine, which has increased its resilience and preparedness despite ongoing war. This involves expertise in rebuilding and renewal, but also unleashing and harnessing people's capacity to innovate. Placemaking in cities and parks has proved highly important for residents' mental strength and adaptability. What can we achieve by acting on these lessons? Which solutions for energy, mobility and material flows are relevant? What could work in a Swedish context?
Meet our panel with extensive experience from Ukraine.
Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard during Almedalsveckan! Forward-looking actors in the built environment sector gather for the fourth consecutive year. No registration is required – we offer a relaxed courtyard setting where you can hear incisive observations and join solution-focused discussions.

content.title: We are building blind
content.description: The need for traceability, control and follow-up is growing. When information gets stuck between stakeholders and stages, deviations are discovered only after causing errors, delays and additional costs. Data creates value only when it is standardised, machine-readable, traceable and interoperable throughout the value chain.
content.extendedDescription:
We seem to be building blind, despite never having had more data.

Deviations are discovered late, quantities do not match and decisions rest on uncertain information. Meanwhile, demands for traceability, climate data and reporting are growing. The question is not whether information is available, but why we do not use it better.

The SBUF-funded project Från BIM till BOM – Obruten digital värdekedja brings industry stakeholders together to challenge current methods and establish a vision for a more coherent process.

How can we create information flows in which errors are immediately visible, transparency increases and we can trust what is built? And how can we ensure data strengthens productivity instead of becoming another administrative layer? These are the questions we raise.

This seminar is for those working in construction, property, design or digital development who want to help shape a more efficient, sustainable industry in an increasingly data-driven world.

content.title: The competition for capital – financing a competitive energy system
content.description: The energy transition requires investment of many billions, but capital hesitates when the rules change. How do political decisions and greater uncertainty affect willingness to invest? What is needed for a stable investment climate for tomorrow's energy system?
content.extendedDescription:
The energy transition requires investment of billions on a scale rarely seen before. Historically, the energy system was built through close interaction between the state and capital, but political uncertainty, geopolitical instability and new risks now challenge that model.

Long-term conditions and clear incentives are crucial for investors. Meanwhile, politicians face pressure to play an active role in developing the energy system and introduce rapid measures against high, volatile electricity prices.

Why have many investors withdrawn from the Swedish market, and how can we reverse the trend? Can politicians create sufficient investment stability while demonstrating decisive action to voters?

This panel brings together investors, energy companies and politicians to discuss financing the energy system. What role should the state play, and how can private billions contribute to a competitive energy system?

content.description: Sweden is heading into an election at a time of profound change. Quick fixes and short-term initiatives are not enough. content.title: PISA 2029 will measure AI literacy – are Swedish schools ready?
content.description: In three years, PISA will begin measuring young people's AI literacy. Meanwhile, the proposed new compulsory school curricula call for restrictive use of digital learning materials and tools. How do these fit together?
content.extendedDescription:
When PISA 2029 takes place, Swedish compulsory school pupils' AI literacy will be measured for the first time. This raises new questions about schools' mission: what knowledge and skills do pupils need to develop to be prepared for the future? And how does this fit with Swedish education policy emphasising restraint in the use of digital tools and learning materials?

This seminar brings together different professional perspectives to discuss what AI literacy means in practice. What consequences do today's choices have for pupils' learning? How are equity and future results affected?
What should school authorities, school leaders and teachers be doing now to prepare themselves and their pupils for PISA 2029?

content.title: AI in schools – who takes responsibility when development outpaces governance?
content.description: AI is changing schools faster than regulations can keep up. Clear national guidelines are lacking, but school providers must act. Scenario-based support for governance, ethics and technology has been developed. How can it help, and whose responsibility is it to lead the way?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is developing rapidly and already affects everyday school life, from learning tools and assessment to administration. Although the school system has been included in Sweden's AI strategy since February 2026, national guidelines on managing AI in schools are lacking. School providers face daily questions about ethics, law and technology choices without national support.
In this vacuum, SKR and Ifous, together with 16 other stakeholders, have developed a web-based support tool built around scenarios and three learning pathways: Governance & Leadership, Ethics & Law and Technology Procurement. The tool launches in June 2026 as an open resource. In parallel, Ifous runs the "AI i utbildning" support process, strengthening teachers' ability to select AI tools on pedagogical grounds.
The seminar demonstrates the tool and discusses responsibilities between the state, municipalities and school providers. Participants receive practical tools to take home and insights into how other municipalities address these issues. The discussion starts from real dilemmas school leaders face daily.
content.subject: Education
speakerTitles: Head of Communications and Social Impact

content.title: Where is Swedish aid heading? Development, choices and consequences
content.description: Swedish aid faces choices: should it primarily reduce poverty or also serve national interests? Amid war, climate crisis and growing needs, priorities affect who receives support and Sweden's role, credibility and responsibility worldwide.
content.extendedDescription:
How is future Swedish aid shaped amid growing global crises and changing political priorities? This conversation invites in-depth dialogue on Sweden's role in international aid, bringing different perspectives on development, direction and priorities together.

It starts from choices shaping aid policy today: balancing poverty reduction with national interests, long-term development with urgent humanitarian action, and broad coverage with concentration. How do these choices affect which countries and groups receive support, and with what results?

Through open, reflective discussion, we explore the consequences of current priorities globally and for Sweden's role, credibility and responsibility internationally. The dialogue allows different voices and aims to build a more nuanced, forward-looking understanding of aid's future.
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Hate, threats, imprisonment – repression against human rights defenders and climate justice activists
content.description: In countries across Europe, individuals are arrested and sentenced to long prison terms after saving people from drowning at sea. Groups fighting for the climate are prosecuted for sabotage, and calls are being made to label rights activism and climate justice activism as terrorism. How did this happen?
content.extendedDescription:
The discussion describes the deterioration in the ability of human rights defenders and climate justice activists to operate in Europe and Sweden today. Companies sue organisations for millions, and individual representatives face threats and hate campaigns. Activists are accused of, and sometimes even convicted of, offences such as people smuggling, espionage, sabotage, extremism or terrorism. We highlight the problem through current cases, with some focus on prosecutions and convictions of asylum rights defenders and people saving lives in the Mediterranean. The discussion will also address situations in which individuals exercising their trade union or political rights to protest and demonstrate are portrayed as security risks and, in some cases, have lost their jobs, as well as the tightening of rules around climate justice activism.
International instruments exist to protect human rights defenders and climate justice activists. What are they, why are they needed, and how are they observed?
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: Civil defence and urban design – how do we build attractive and resilient living environments?
content.description: How can we build attractive environments that combine sustainable development with preparedness for crisis and war? New approaches to designed environments at neighbourhood level, with local resilience and public spaces that can be mobilised for critical societal functions. What strengthens our social and civil capabilities in the built environment?
content.extendedDescription:
With greater pressure on total defence, the built environment sector needs to rethink urban design. This involves aspects of the physical environment: evacuation routes, shelters, multifunctional spaces, building conversion, energy supply and alternative modes of transport. Our social capital, neighbourhood cooperation and local expertise are also very important. Can the transition to circular cities strengthen civil defence capabilities?
For the 4th consecutive year, join discussions at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard in Visby, with leading representatives of the built environment sector, the public sector and urban design. In an era of increased vulnerability, we jointly frame the big questions and the strategies required.
No registration is required – we offer a relaxed courtyard setting where you can hear incisive observations and take part in solution-focused discussions. Together, we create sustainable, resilient communities. Welcome!

content.title: A meeting place for democracy's defenders
content.description: Swedish democracy remains strong, but faces challenges. Those who refuse to accept this development and instead want to strengthen, protect and deepen democracy therefore need to come together.
content.extendedDescription:
Efficiency drives, rapid decisions, casting suspicion on professionals and an increasingly harsh tone have created a social climate in which many feel growing concern. When threats, hatred and a culture of silence take hold and experts are questioned, democracy's foundations risk being weakened.

As the trade union for those working on behalf of the state, ST has a responsibility to stand up for a strong and open democracy. Together with others, we want to explore, deepen and defend the principles that keep democracy alive – in public authorities, public debate and people's everyday lives.

At this meeting place, we bring together everyone who sees the worrying signs and wants to contribute to a different direction. We listen to insightful perspectives, share experiences and discuss how we can strengthen democracy together where it is actually practised.

content.title: Circular value creation: transforming buildings and reuse along the value chain
content.description: A shift is under way in how we value what is already built. Inventories of cultural heritage values, material resources and climate investments, and avoiding waste, are becoming central to a circular economy. Meanwhile, the value chain is changing around guarantees, take-back schemes and logistics for circular product flows.
content.extendedDescription: Which actors manage value where, upstream and downstream in the value chain? What characterises an architecture of transformation, where buildings and construction products are designed for longer lives, flexibility, disassembly and modification? EU requirements for digital product passports will soon be introduced, and the Ecodesign Directive raises repairability requirements. Inventories can collect information on existing materials digitally, linked through ReUseApp as reuse data directly in BIM models. Data on reused materials becomes searchable, comparable and traceable to better manage the value of what already exists. For the fourth consecutive year, forward-looking actors in the built environment sector gather at Omställningsarenan, Sweco's courtyard, during Almedalsveckan! This moderated roundtable in fishbowl format is organised with Tarkett. A group representing different perspectives on the value chain shares incisive observations in a solution-focused discussion about circular value creation for buildings and the construction product value chain.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Teachers and AI: who gives them the tools when guidelines are missing?
content.description: AI has quickly become part of everyday school life, but many teachers still lack support, guidance and confidence in using it, especially with pupils. Meanwhile, differences between schools and education providers are growing. What happens to equity when development proceeds at different speeds?
content.extendedDescription:
Novus's annual survey of 530 compulsory school teachers, commissioned by Dustin, shows how quickly AI has moved from experimentation to an everyday school tool. Seven in ten teachers now use AI at work, mainly to create teaching materials and plan lessons. Just over half feel that AI improves teaching, and more feel confident with the technology than a year ago.

Yet AI is still used cautiously in teaching. Only 31 per cent of teachers have worked with AI together with pupils. Many lack time, pedagogical support and clear guidelines for safe, responsible use.

The results are presented for the first time at the seminar. The panel discusses how schools can move from uncertainty to confident AI use, and what is needed for AI to strengthen teaching without increasing inequality between pupils and schools.

content.title: Building vocational education that delivers employable skills
content.description: Skills shortages are well documented, yet many vocational programmes still do not lead to jobs. The problem is rarely the length of education, but how learning is organised. The question is how structure, progression and links to working life determine whether education actually becomes employable competence.
content.extendedDescription:
Skills shortages are intensely debated, but responses often focus on volume rather than how vocational education is organised to lead to jobs. Some vocational programmes do not provide participants with the skills employers actually need. The problem is rarely time, but how education is organised.

This seminar starts from a clear question: why do some vocational programmes lead to jobs while others do not? It focuses on how structure, progression and links to working life determine quality, pace and employability.

The discussion draws on a coherent model of vocational education already used in practice, showing how learning can be organised more effectively without lowering requirements, safety standards or the professional role. The perspective broadens from individual programmes to what is needed for consistent quality and scalability across larger systems.

The event is a structured discussion with concrete examples and clearly defined themes.
content.subject: Education

content.title: How school meals save the world – and how Sweden can contribute
content.description: Amid major humanitarian crises and challenges for the development sector, there is also good news: school meal programmes continue to expand and develop.
content.extendedDescription:
In a global development context with many large-scale challenges, school meals really are a superhero! Good school meal programmes improve education and pupils' concentration, promote health, strengthen children's nutrition and support local economies and food systems. School meals also matter for preparedness in humanitarian crises and have life-changing effects, especially for girls. In short, school meal programmes can save the world!

WFP's goal is bold but clear: every child should have access to a nutritious school meal by 2030! Although 466 million children worldwide are covered by school meal programmes, more than 100 million children and young people still go without. Why, and how can the international community, including humanitarian and development actors, expand these programmes widely?
How does WFP work with school meals in the forgotten crisis in Sudan? And what role can Sweden play in global school meal efforts?

content.title: Future energy scenarios: their development and impact on spatial planning
content.description: The energy system relies on long-term planning and future energy scenarios. These have developed enormously in recent years, with ambitious assumptions and rising estimates of future demand.
content.extendedDescription:
Over the past 40 years, electricity consumption in Sweden has remained stable at around 130–140 TWh per year. Continuous energy efficiency improvements have met additional demand. But we now face a transition in which large parts of industry and transport will be electrified, and a narrative of doubling electricity use has become established. As Energimyndigheten releases new scenarios, the range of outcomes has continued to rise and widen, with further scenarios based on even more ambitious assumptions. Yet electrification has not taken off and forecasts are being pushed back. Meanwhile, factors such as the energy crisis, demographic change, faltering investment and more ambitious efficiency measures add further uncertainty.
This seminar addresses questions including: what assumptions underpin Energimyndigheten's long-term scenarios? Is the government's planned increase compatible with our energy policy goals? How should we plan energy provision in the face of current uncertainty?

content.title: One in three Swedes is uncertain about EU membership: why?
content.description:
A democratic society welcomes participation. How does EU centralisation affect public participation? What opportunities exist to exert influence within the EU?
Which EU-related issues feel most relevant ahead of the 2026 election? What would a forthcoming constitutional amendment mean, for example?
content.extendedDescription:
According to SCB's latest survey in June 2025, 11 per cent of the electorate is ‘against’ and 23 per cent ‘uncertain about’ Swedish EU membership. These figures represent around 3 million Swedes' opposition and doubts.
Turnout in the 2024 European election fell from 55% in 2019 to 53%, indicating declining public interest in the EU as an institution. What has happened to expectations? Is today's EU what we voted on in the 1994 referendum? How can we respond to developments?

The discussion starts from three approaches to Swedish EU membership:

• Accept and embrace the EU's current development.
• Seek to influence its direction through reform.
• Leave the EU and establish corresponding cooperation along the lines of Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

Folkrörelsen Nej till EU (FNEU) follows up, investigates and discusses EU membership's effects in a democratic spirit without party-political affiliation.

content.title: Who takes responsibility for cleaning up the atmosphere with carbon credits – companies, the state or the EU?
content.description: Carbon credits (CDR, Carbon Dioxide Removals) are shifting from a climate tool to a strategic market issue. Companies buy credits to strengthen their climate plans, investors demand net-zero strategies and the EU is building a new regulatory framework for certifying negative emissions.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is testing reverse auctions to purchase permanent negative emissions – but without a long-term plan for what happens afterwards. The result is a rapidly growing but fragmented market in which three actors are trying to take the lead:

Companies – net emitters:
They have current and historical emissions. They want to use carbon credits and CDRs to strengthen competitiveness, win business and invest in new technology – but need clear rules and quality assurance.

The state:
It is testing auctions and pilot programmes, but has not yet defined the role Sweden should play in the European CDR market.

The EU:
It is developing certification frameworks and discussing joint purchasing programmes, which could reshape the entire market and affect opportunities for Swedish companies.

The big question is therefore:
Who should take the lead in building a credible and competitive market for negative emissions – companies, the state or the EU – and what is the next step in its development?

content.title: Should Sweden build carbon dioxide infrastructure for 3 million tonnes – or 30?
content.description: Sweden needs a clear carbon capture strategy specifying the capacity we should build for. The country's biogenic emissions exceed 30 million tonnes per year, but policy is based on around 3 million tonnes – a gap that risks steering the entire system in the wrong direction.
content.extendedDescription:
BioCCUS, Bioenergy Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage, means capturing carbon dioxide at the emission source and either storing it permanently or using it in industrial processes.

Scaling up CCUS requires a coordinated structure for capturing, handling and transporting carbon dioxide. This means solutions that work for both large and small operators, and targeted support that builds shared infrastructure rather than individual projects. Such support would make many more projects possible, particularly for operators with smaller volumes who otherwise risk being left out.

Storage and transport operators are planning for large, steady flows, requiring Sweden to design its future infrastructure for considerably larger volumes than those currently under discussion. If we build too small, we risk bottlenecks, higher costs and a market that never gets going. The central question for debate therefore remains: should Sweden build carbon dioxide infrastructure for 3 million tonnes – or 30?

content.title: New perspectives on local democracy and local energy production
content.description: Renewable electricity is crucial for jobs and welfare, but is often held back by local opposition. How are our views of energy projects formed – and how can better knowledge and more perspectives contribute to better-informed decisions?
content.extendedDescription:
Industry's transition requires more renewable electricity. Without it, investment, jobs and ultimately welfare are at risk. At the same time, energy projects face local opposition often characterised by limited participation and social misconceptions.
The ways people influence one another – through norms, conversations and local opinion – play a major role in how energy projects are perceived. Yet today's consultation processes primarily engage nearby residents, while other perspectives, particularly those of young people, are rarely heard.
Through Almedalsveckans Demokratiskola, engaged young people gain knowledge, tools and the ability to understand and influence societal issues in a democratic context. In this seminar, they contribute their perspectives and highlight both shortcomings in current processes and opportunities for more inclusive approaches.
The seminar explores how we can strengthen knowledge, broaden dialogue and make more legitimate decisions about the energy systems of the future.

content.title: Is Almedalsveckan sustainable, or does it leave a hangover?
content.description: The need for lively, sustainable and visionary meeting places has never been greater. But how are Almedalsveckan and other Swedish events really doing? Are they sustainable environmentally and in terms of democracy and fairness, or does the hangover outweigh the benefits?
content.extendedDescription:
Rearmament, climate change and threats to democracy create anxiety and risk eroding hope for the future. Meeting places such as Almedalsveckan can generate visions, energy and hope as foundations for a safer, more sustainable Sweden, but how well are we succeeding? Through our movement Baksmällan, we invite sustainability and event experts, KISAM – Världens ungdomar and others to scrutinise Almedalen. Last year's focus was diversity; this year's is racism and discrimination. Findings and proposals for improvement are presented during the week's final hours.
As one of the week's final events, like a painkiller for a hangover, we get on our high horses, sum up our impressions and ask: are we reaching WHERE we want, and WHO we want? What should we continue, what should we improve, and how? Together with YOU, we sum up and develop proposals to make us even better. Join in and share your views: your voice counts!
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Energy preparedness now – solutions for clean energy, flexible grids and energy-positive districts
content.description: The global situation requires new approaches to reduce dependence on oil prices and strengthen energy security. Which design and system solutions can be scaled up: buildings with island operation, solar power and battery storage, waste heat recovery, balancing electricity grids or bio-CCS?
content.extendedDescription:
What concrete scenarios exist as we transition to robust, redundant and resilient energy systems? A local energy transition is under way in our cities, developing attractive places with more resilient energy supplies. Homes, blocks and neighbourhoods are moving from passive electricity customers to active parts of the energy system.
Greater sharing, digital control, electrification, solar and wind power, battery storage and waste heat recovery are creating a new, more decentralised energy landscape. These solutions provide access to cleaner energy and a vision of energy justice.
Meanwhile, today's electricity grids, historically built for a centralised, one-way system, are being challenged. Suppose this transformation were possible: what would it take?
Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard in Visby during Almedalsveckan! For the fourth consecutive year, forward-looking stakeholders in the built environment come together. You are welcome to participate.

content.description: Sweden's competitiveness depends on a skilled workforce with strong digital and AI skills. What does Sweden need to do to prepare tomorrow's workers?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is expected to transform the economy and working life in the coming years. For Sweden to strengthen its competitiveness, it needs widespread digital skills, cutting-edge AI expertise and an education system that prepares people for a new era. content.title: How does the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum affect Sweden's reception of refugees?
content.description: The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum has now begun to apply throughout the EU, and migration is largely governed by European legislation. How will the change affect future reception of people seeking protection, what does the new screening involve, and how will the new reception and return centres work?
content.extendedDescription:
Join a seminar exploring the historic change as legislation on seeking protection becomes common across the EU, from Spain to Sweden. This major transition affects every part of the protection process, from applications through investigation, decisions and return. During the seminar you will learn more; during the webinar you will learn, among other things, about:
• Why the migration pact is being introduced and what it aims to achieve
• The Screening Regulation and new checks at the external border
• The new asylum process and how it differs from the current system
• How the new reception and return centres will operate

content.title: Military communications security – knowledge that has yet to reach civilian society
content.description: For decades, the military has protected communications and command systems against interception, interference and electromagnetic pulses. This knowledge is proven. But as the same threats now reach civilian agencies and critical infrastructure, both expertise and tools are lacking. The gap is growing.
content.extendedDescription:
The boundary between military communications security and civilian preparedness is no longer clear. Hostile actors use the same methods against civilian targets that were previously directed only at military ones: jammers, IMSI catchers, electromagnetic pulses and remote control of devices that should be offline.
The discussion connects military experience to civilian application: what works in the field, what can be transferred and where civilian society's responsibility begins.
An open, question-led discussion. Held outside BLCKR's Signalskugga, a signal-blocking tent in Visby harbour where all communication is cut off. Coffee is served.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: NIS2 requires you to protect the room, not just the system: is your agency ready?
content.description: The EU's new cybersecurity law, NIS2, requires an all-hazards approach, including protection of the physical environment housing IT systems. Most agencies focus on firewalls and access control. But signal leakage and vulnerable equipment are rarely addressed. The law and the future demand more.
content.extendedDescription:
NIS2 entered into force in Sweden on 1 January 2025. The directive requires organisations to approach security from an all-hazards perspective. This means organisations, particularly government agencies, must not only apply digital safeguards but also protect the physical environment housing IT systems and critical equipment. In practice, this entails requirements for continuity management, protection against electromagnetic interference and signal isolation.

The discussion includes a live demonstration of what an unprepared office environment looks like from a signal perspective: which devices are visible, what is transmitting and what this means for an agency under pressure.

An open, question-led discussion held outdoors beside BLCKR's Signalskugga, a signal-blocking tent in Visby harbour. Coffee will be served.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Future supply of goods – from efficient to robust flows
content.description: What happens when chips do not arrive from Asia, medicines get stuck in port or grain cannot be transported? Just-in-time no longer works. We need new solutions allowing energy, food and medicine to be produced, stored and transported securely, even in turbulent times.
content.extendedDescription:
When the pandemic struck, factories stopped. When the Suez Canal was blocked, everything was delayed. We now know global supply chains are vulnerable. The solution? More local production and smarter logistics. Think concretely: energy companies securing local energy. Food producers making and storing food regionally so shop shelves remain stocked in a crisis. Pharmaceutical companies bringing critical medicine production home. How can we plan factories, warehouses and freight terminals close to consumers? How can railways function when lorries stop? These questions are debated here.

Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard in Visby during Almedalsveckan! For the fourth consecutive year, forward-looking built-environment stakeholders gather. No registration is required: enjoy a relaxed courtyard setting with incisive observations and take part in solution-oriented discussions. Together, we create sustainable, resilient societies. content.title: What do we get for our healthcare spending – why are patients' different needs not being met?
content.description: What does putting the patient first really mean when needs differ greatly? How can healthcare balance person-centred care, efficiency and equity, and do we need more developed organisational triage to meet the needs of different patient groups?
content.extendedDescription:
The patient should be the focus, but who is this patient? Often there are many different individuals with varying needs and preferences, even within the same medical condition. Topics include tailoring care to target groups, person-centred care, general guidelines and the advantages and disadvantages of freedom of choice. How can we meet the needs of expert patients, patients with rare conditions, patients with common, straightforward needs and very ill patients within the same service – and should we really do so everywhere? We are good at medical triage, but can we also develop organisational triage that enables appropriate individualisation while making services more efficient?

The seminar is part of Arena Tillsammans, the meeting place for healthcare's major systemic issues during Almedalsveckan.

content.title: The invisible threat — AI, OT security and espionage we do not see
content.description: Society is becoming increasingly digital and connected, and therefore more vulnerable. How can the public sector and businesses harness technology's opportunities without losing control?
content.extendedDescription:
Panel 1: Secure AI transformation in municipalities
AI creates major opportunities for the public sector, but also raises important questions about information security, responsibility and protection of digital assets. We discuss how Sweden's municipalities can take the next step in AI transformation safely and sustainably.

Panel 2: OT security and protection of critical infrastructure
Operational Technology, OT, controls everything from buildings and physical flows to critical societal functions. As these systems become connected, vulnerability increases. We highlight today's threats and discuss what organisations need to do to strengthen resilience.

Panel 3: Digital Espionage – The Invisible Threat and What We Can Do
Digital espionage often happens silently, but can have far-reaching consequences for businesses, organisations and national security. We discuss today's threat landscape and the measures needed to detect, understand and counter unseen actors.

content.title: Scale up – use medical technology for equitable care, shorter waiting lists and stronger competitiveness
content.description: Sweden faces societal challenges involving healthcare waiting lists, unequal care and an ageing population. At the same time, we need more growth and stronger competitiveness. Medical technology contributes solutions in these areas, but barriers prevent scaling up.
content.extendedDescription:
Medical technology enables early detection, safer treatments and more personalised care. For cancer patients, it is part of every step from diagnosis to rehabilitation. For healthcare services, it increases efficiency and frees up time through digital solutions, hospital care at home and self-monitoring, while strengthening patient safety. The sector is important for competitiveness: 60 per cent of Swedish life science companies work in medical technology.

Sweden is one of Europe's leading countries for medtech patent applications. When the medical technology sector grows here, Sweden grows and strengthens Europe. When medical innovations are used in healthcare, patients, healthcare services and society benefit.

But barriers remain. What is needed to scale up the use of medical technology for more equitable care, shorter waiting lists and stronger competitiveness?

content.title: Municipal IT and operational systems based on open source for greater digital sovereignty
content.description: Today, Sweden's municipalities depend more or less entirely on systems from American tech giants in their day-to-day operations. But what happens if those companies cannot be relied on, and what alternatives exist for municipalities that want greater independence and less lock-in?
content.extendedDescription:
American software suppliers have long dominated the Swedish market, not least in Sweden's municipalities. Much of their day-to-day work depends on services and platforms over which the municipalities themselves have limited control. This makes the question increasingly pressing: what happens if these companies can no longer provide the services we depend on, change their terms unilaterally or are affected by geopolitical decisions?
This discussion explores whether municipalities have an alternative route to greater digital sovereignty through solutions such as open source and open technical standards. Are there concrete examples of organisations that have chosen this path? What are the lessons, and is it even possible?

Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard during Almedalsveckan! No registration is required – we offer a relaxed courtyard setting where you can hear incisive observations and take part in solution-focused discussions.

content.title: Young people's influence in construction: self-organisation, networks and activism
content.description: As a young person, it is easy to feel powerless about the direction our future is taking. Construction accounts for 22% of Sweden's domestic carbon dioxide emissions. content.extendedDescription:
Seminar and shared reflection.

In August, a climate election booth built by StuCAN will be displayed in central Gothenburg. Created in cooperation with Gothenburg's climate movement, it has enabled young architecture and engineering students to exert influence and practise their professions before graduating.

We have a responsibility to act not only as private individuals but also through our professional knowledge. Together, we explore how self-organisation can create change, solidarity and hope.

Throughout history, the wish to influence and make a difference without access to money or senior professional positions has forced young people to do the only thing they can: take action to gain attention. Non-profit associations with limited resources share this experience.

content.title: How a hard-to-love property from the 1970s was given new life through reuse
content.description: What should we do with office buildings from the 1960s and 1970s: too young to merit protection, too old to be considered modern? A completed project shows that reuse and respect for a building's original qualities can deliver both a low climate footprint and a stronger identity.
content.extendedDescription:
Office buildings from the 1960s and 1970s are demolished or rebuilt without regard for what already exists, even though reuse and preservation can deliver major climate benefits and retain unique qualities. The "hard-to-love" risks disappearing, despite possessing values we cannot recreate.
In the Vi på hörnet project in central Göteborg, Semrén & Månsson Arkitekter, together with Alecta Fastigheter and RO-Gruppen, transformed a building from the 1960s/1970s, taking its own character and period qualities as their starting point. The result: 10,000 m² of renewed office space and climate savings of 183,000 kg CO₂e.
During the discussion, we share practical lessons about reuse as a strategy, collaboration between architect, property owner and contractor, measuring climate benefits, and what is needed for circular construction to become the norm rather than the exception.
The discussion is open and requires no prior knowledge. You are welcome whether you work in construction and property or have a general interest in sustainable urban development.

content.title: From Nordic innovation to global impact
content.description: The Nordic countries offer strong conditions for innovation, but new ideas do not automatically become successful products and services in the market. How can we better connect research, innovation and commercialisation?
content.extendedDescription:
EU competitiveness discussions identify weak commercialisation and scaling of new technology as one of Europe's biggest challenges. The Nordic countries are among the world's most innovative, but small domestic markets mean that even strong ideas often stall before reaching international scale. Does the Nordic region face similar barriers to those identified at EU level: fragmented markets, complex regulations, a shortage of venture capital and weak demand?

From a Nordic perspective, the aim is to improve conditions for innovations to scale up faster and reach international markets.

The discussion between Nordic stakeholders will identify and highlight the region's most important barriers and clarify where Nordic cooperation can add value beyond national and regional initiatives.

content.title: Medical evacuation in Ukraine - What does it take to save lives?
content.description: Medical evacuation in Ukraine is no longer simply about moving wounded soldiers to safety. Drones, precision strikes and constant surveillance have transformed battlefield conditions, requiring evacuation vehicles to evolve continuously.
content.extendedDescription:
Medical evacuation in Ukraine is no longer simply about transporting wounded soldiers to safety. Drones, precision strikes and constant surveillance have fundamentally changed how evacuation missions are conducted and what vehicles are needed to survive.
As the battlefield evolves, civilian pickups, vans and SUVs are continuously adapted with new protection, evacuation layouts and practical solutions based on frontline experience. What worked a few months ago may no longer be effective today.
In this session, Ukrainian combat medic and Tac Med North instructor Oleksandr will share firsthand insights from helping convert more than 230 vehicles for medical evacuation and frontline support. Through real examples, including projects supported by HUG, participants will learn how battlefield needs drive innovation and how volunteers, engineers and military personnel work together to save lives.
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Where are the limits of digitalisation?
content.description: How digitalisation and new, sometimes mandatory standards can create efficiency and societal benefits for businesses while risking obsolescence or market distortion, and where the limits lie for public steering of innovation.
content.extendedDescription:
In debates about business, freedom and deregulation are often presented as the opposite of red tape and compulsion. But digitalisation challenges this dichotomy. New standards, sometimes mandatory, can create enormous benefits for businesses and society. More efficient reporting to authorities and e-invoicing, for example, can free up time and resources.

Yet risks remain. Initiatives can quickly become outdated or drive developments that suit political priorities rather than companies. There are also distortions affecting specific industries. Where should the line be drawn? Can the public sector genuinely steer digital development constructively, and where does it go wrong?

In this breakfast seminar, we discuss the balance between rules and innovation, opportunities and pitfalls, and how digitalisation can become a tool rather than an obstacle.

Breakfast is served.

content.title: The great inheritance shift in the single-family housing market – a national change with local consequences
content.description: The great inheritance shift could redraw the single-family housing market. What happens when 300,000 houses change hands – to housing chains, prices, planning and housing policy?
content.extendedDescription: Over the next 20 years, more than 300,000 single-family homes are expected to change hands through inheritance and, in many cases, come onto the market instead of staying in the family. That is more homes than have been built in Sweden in just over three decades. As large numbers of single-family homes gradually reach the market, this could change the conditions for housing chains, price formation and housing provision in many municipalities. Our stock of single-family homes, currently largely occupied by older people, is likely to gain younger residents. What does this great inheritance shift mean for the single-family housing market, local planning and housing policy as a whole?

content.title: A national museum card – the key to greater access and stronger cultural policy?
content.description: Could a shared museum card help lower barriers to culture, broaden audiences and strengthen museums' role in democracy? And what cultural policy choices arise if a museum card is to become a tool for increased
content.extendedDescription:
Sveriges Museer has received government funding to explore, with an open mind, the opportunities and challenges of a national Swedish museum card. During Kultur i Almedalen 2026, the first interim report from the feasibility study will be presented, with in-depth case studies analysing the potential effects of a museum card on accessibility, participation and museums' long-term sustainability throughout the country.

Could a shared museum card help lower barriers to culture, broaden audiences and strengthen museums' role in democracy? How would it affect the relationship between the state, regions, municipalities and civil society? And what cultural policy choices arise if a museum card is to become a tool for better achievement of objectives and equal access to culture?

Participants include Sveriges Museer's new Chair Cajsa Lagerkvist, Secretary General Gunnar Ardelius, and Jaakko Rytsölä and Perttu Rytsölä, the report authors, who have extensive experience of developing the Finnish museum card. Moderator: Sharon Jåma.

content.title: Can you build a voter base through housing?
content.description: Detached houses mean right-wing votes and rentals left-wing votes? Hardly. Urban voters reluctant to vote right dominate big-city tenant-owned apartments, and detached-house neighbourhoods are far from ideologically uniform. What role does housing really play in party sympathies and voting patterns in a complex electorate?
content.extendedDescription: Suburban detached housing produces centre-right voters, while renters vote left. Is it really that simple? Housing has become an engine of new political divides cutting across traditional bloc politics. Urban voters reluctant to vote right dominate expensive city apartments, and detached-house neighbourhoods are far from ideologically uniform. For those excluded from home ownership, housing can symbolise political exclusion and a sense of failure, driving sympathies towards populist movements. What role does housing actually play in party sympathies and voting patterns in Sweden's increasingly complex electorate?

content.title: Sweden's image and the shift in security policy: perspectives on NATO membership
content.description: How does the image of Sweden, at home and abroad, change when long-standing military non-alignment is replaced by NATO membership? How is Swedish security policy affected by an increasingly uncertain international order and a deteriorating security situation?
content.extendedDescription:
Some of the chapter authors of “Är Sverige säkert nu? Perspektiv på Nato och svensk säkerhetspolitik” (edited by Linus Hagström) discuss Sweden's shift in security policy.
For two centuries, Sweden was associated with neutrality and military non-alignment – a policy that contributed significantly to the country's self-image and international identity. How has this reorientation been justified and legitimised in public? How have emotions, narratives and gender perspectives been used to understand and justify the shift in security policy? What does it mean that the feminist foreign policy was withdrawn in connection with Sweden's accession to NATO, and how can this be understood in relation to the new security policy direction? Finally, how should we view Sweden's security just over two years after joining NATO, at a time when the United States' long-term commitment to European security can increasingly be questioned, and amid a new international disorder?

content.title: Welfare crime – a growing societal problem requiring shared responsibility
content.description: Welfare crime is a serious threat to our shared welfare systems. When public funds are misused or obtained through irregularities, resources are drained from schools, healthcare and social care. For municipalities and regions, this means financial losses and reduced trust in the public sector.
content.extendedDescription:
How extensive is welfare crime in municipalities and regions today, what methods are used and how is it developing over time? Effective prevention requires knowledge of the scale of the problem and an understanding of risks and vulnerabilities within one's own organisation.

This seminar examines the development of welfare crime in municipalities and regions. You will receive an up-to-date picture of how it appears in practice and which areas are particularly vulnerable. We also highlight auditing's role in revealing risks, examining governance and controls, and contributing to more systematic prevention. Concrete examples from municipalities and regions provide experience of how organisations can strengthen their work against welfare crime before harm occurs.

The seminar is aimed at elected representatives, managers, auditors and others wishing to strengthen their work to protect welfare and ensure public resources are used properly.

content.title: 25 years of crises: what has liberalism been doing?
content.description: A review of liberalism's intellectual development during the first quarter-century of the 2000s. How has the ideology navigated crises, innovations, wars and a pandemic, and perhaps its own fading existence?
content.extendedDescription:
The first quarter-century of the 2000s is said to belong to populists and anti-democrats. There is talk of conservatism's return and the radicalisation of the left. Liberalism, by contrast, is widely regarded as being in crisis.

But is that really true? Liberal thought over the past quarter-century tells another story.
The anthology ‘A Liberal Canon’ collects the 2000s' most important texts for liberalism. It shows how liberalism has shaped, and been shaped by, financial and migration crises, the war on terrorism, right-wing populism's rise, increased prosperity, technological advances and much else.

Liberal kanon was produced by Timbro förlag in collaboration with Liberal Debatt, featuring texts by Anne Applebaum, Karl-Ove Knausgård, Johan Norberg and Boualem Sansal, among others.

content.title: From protest to project — managing public opinion in urban development
content.description: More and more projects face opposition, appeals or lost momentum. This slows construction, affects investment and damages trust in planning. How can public opinion be addressed in ways that strengthen both democratic influence and feasibility, and how can earlier engagement reduce the risk of deadlock?
content.extendedDescription:
More and more projects face opposition, lose momentum or become stuck. But resistance does not necessarily mean a project is wrong; it may equally indicate inadequate engagement.

This seminar starts from two concrete cases in Uppsala illustrating both successes and setbacks in managing public opinion. They provide the basis for a panel discussion on democracy, legitimacy, feasibility and the importance of early engagement.

Experience shows that conflicts often arise when planning starts at the wrong end, with volumes and development rather than a place's conditions, qualities and potential. When people are invited in only after proposals have been formulated, the process risks becoming deadlocked.

We discuss what is needed to move from reactive management of public opinion to proactive co-creation.

content.title: The bank as coach or custodian? How to win Gen Z's trust in the financial market of the future
content.description: The financial sector faces a generational shift that challenges traditional customer relationship models. How are the economy and financial loyalty affected when tomorrow's most important customer group no longer trusts the established system?
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar, we present insights from SKI and discuss the paradox that Gen Z demands more guidance than any other generation while trusting themselves more than their bank. Data from SKI's report ‘Young Customers' Expectations of the Financial Sector’ shows that the industry faces a major transition. Fully 48% of Gen Z want proactive contact at important life events, compared with just 16% of Gen X. The younger generation sees the bank as a partner in realising dreams rather than merely somewhere to keep money.
Yet one in four young customers would choose a different bank today if given the chance.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: Orphan medicines in the election – from promises to solutions
content.description: Inadequate access to orphan medicines has serious consequences for patients with rare conditions. Ahead of the election, the question comes to a head: how can political ambitions become concrete reforms that ensure equitable care and strengthen Sweden as a research nation?
content.extendedDescription:
Access to orphan medicines is central, often life-changing, for people with rare conditions. During the spring, debate about access to orphan medicines and Sweden's role as a research nation has intensified. New US pharmaceutical policy is changing the landscape, access to orphan medicines remains low by international standards, and Sweden faces challenges in life science.

The election takes place in September. Voters often rank healthcare among the most important political issues. Kommissionen för innovativa särläkemedel is now taking a new approach, launching its own election manifesto with reform proposals for the coming electoral term.

How can the trend be reversed? What changes are needed in the short and long term? And what are politicians prepared to do? Patients, relatives, experts and business representatives meet politicians in one of Almedalen's most important discussions.

content.title: From waste targets to the classroom — put food waste on the timetable
content.description: How do we achieve the EU's food waste targets in practice? Children's eating habits are shaped at school every day, while large quantities of food are thrown away in Sweden. Putting food waste on the timetable can combine education, sustainability and behaviour change where it makes the greatest difference: in the classroom.
content.extendedDescription:
In 2025, the EU adopted binding food waste targets. Agenda 2030 calls for halving waste at the consumer level. Despite measures taken, we will not reach these targets.

One in five portions in public kitchens is thrown away. Food waste cost SEK 370 million in 2024. We urge children to conserve the planet's resources but fail to set a good example.

Real change requires a broader perspective centred on knowledge of the food system, behaviours and values. Schools are a unique setting where these three can meet and future eating habits are shaped. Learning for sustainable development, sustainable food systems and practical everyday situations can be connected here.

Everyone has a relationship with food, and therefore with food waste. By increasing understanding of food's value, we can strengthen respect for raw ingredients and take steps to reduce waste.
content.subject: Food
